## Scope

This chapter states which genes should enter a DeCovarT reference built
from single-cell data, and why. It holds the theory: what the genes are
for, the selection strategies of the literature, four tiers of
selection, and the statistical tests and tail bounds behind them
[@gaspard-boulincCelltypeDeconvolutionMethods2025;
@avilacobosComputationalDeconvolutionTranscriptomics2018]. The
reference considered here is a single-cell experiment on one specimen.
Cross-cell consistency (tier ii, @sec-fs-consistency) uses that
reference alone; cross-platform consistency (tier iii,
@sec-fs-cross-platform) also needs a bulk sample that matches it.
Cross-sample consistency, references from other technologies,
dependent cells and covariance-driven selection are perspectives
(@sec-perspectives). The application to a real reference (filters as
applied, settings, rank tables, code) is in the feature-selection
chapter of the reproducibility book. Strategies compared on simulated
references are in [Appendix S6](S6-feature-screening-scenario.html).
Marker-based abundance scores (enrichment modules) are out of scope
[@aranXCellDigitallyPortraying2017].
:::

**Local symbols.** $C=\sum_jC_j$ is the number of reference cells in
one time slot, and $j(c)$ is the label of cell $c$. $v_{gj}$ is the
$g$-th diagonal entry of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$. A gene panel is written
$\mathcal{G}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,G\}$. In the review, $\mu_{gj}$ is the
mean of gene $g$ in type $j$ on the scale of the method at hand,
$u_{gj}$ its type share and $k$ a rank (@eq-gini). In the count models,
$m_{gc}=\operatorname{E}(x_{gc})$ is the mean of gene $g$ in cell $c$,
$V(m)=m+m^{2}/\psi_g$ the negative-binomial (NB) variance function,
$\mathcal{D}_g(M)$ the deviance of model $M$, $\Lambda_g$ the
likelihood-ratio statistic, $R^{2}_{D,g}$ the deviance explained,
$r_{gc}$ the raw Pearson residual, $r^{\mathrm{SP}}_{gc}$ the
standardised one, $\hat\phi_g$ the Pearson dispersion and $h_{gc}$ the
leverage of cell $c$ (@sec-sctransform, @sec-fs-leverage). For the
bulk filter, $\tilde\mu_{gj}$ is the expected count of gene $g$ in one
cell of type $j$, $\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}$ its average over the $C_j$
reference cells, $\sigma^{2}_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}+\tilde\mu_{gj}^{2}/\psi_g$
the per-cell NB variance, $\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g$ the distance of the
bulk to the range of the reference means, $D_{gi}$ the plug-in
discrepancy, $D^{b}_{gi}$ the discrepancy after dividing the bulk by a
plug-in platform ratio $\hat b_g=\tilde b_ge^{\varepsilon_g}$ with
$v_g=\operatorname{Var}\varepsilon_g$, $L_g$ the mean transcript length,
$h_g$ the leverage of gene $g$ and $\tau_g^{2}$ its
residual variance, $S_M$ the standardised sum over a gene module $M$,
$K_D(u)$ the cumulant generating function of $D$ with argument $u$, and
$\chi_G$ the number of classes of a colouring of a gene graph
(@sec-fs-range-tail). $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_4$ are the parameters of the
sub-exponential properties, and $\gamma,\gamma'$ absolute constants
(@nte-fs-subexp, @nte-fs-bernstein). $B$ is the number of permutations
(@sec-fs-calibration).

::: {#wrn-fs-estimand .callout-warning}
## What the genes are for

The target is a set of genes that makes the reference moments
$(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})$ estimable and
informative about $\boldsymbol{p}$. This is not population-level
differential expression, for two reasons.

- **One specimen.** The reference is one technical scRNA-seq
  experiment. Its cells are draws from one specimen, not biological
  replicates, so every $p$-value below calibrates a *screen inside that
  specimen*. Treating cells as replicates of a population contrast
  inflates the false discoveries
  [@zimmermanPracticalSolutionPseudoreplication2021;
  @squairConfrontingFalseDiscoveries2021;
  @crowellMuscatDetectsSubpopulationspecific2020]. Only the within-donor
  covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ is estimable; the between-donor
  part needs $R\ge2$ donors
  ([2.1](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-one-replicate)).
- **Labels are given.** A test of the type effect is valid only if the
  labels were fixed before the statistic is computed. Labels obtained by
  clustering the same matrix make the test anti-conservative
  (post-clustering inference, González-Delgado et al. 2025)
  [TODO-cite: González-Delgado et al. 2025, post-clustering inference; key gonzalezDelgadoPostclusteringInference2025 exists in the book bib only]{.highlight}.

Selection proceeds in four tiers (@fig-fs-tiers):

1. quality control, prior-knowledge markers and a presence gate
   (@sec-fs-qc);
2. cross-cell consistency: tests of the type effect used as a gate,
   then an effect-size rank (@sec-fs-consistency);
3. cross-platform consistency between the reference and a matched bulk:
   influence diagnostics and a bulk filter (@sec-fs-cross-platform);
4. down-weighting by the model instead of removal (@sec-fs-weighting).

Tiers (i) to (iii) are filters; tier (iv) is part of the likelihood.
Feature selection as a pre-modelling filter has the usual caveats
[@guyonIntroductionVariableFeature2003]: it is a proposal, to be
checked by out-of-sample deconvolution error
([S6](S6-feature-screening-scenario.html#sec-cv-selection)).
:::

# Review of gene-selection strategies used by deconvolution algorithms {#sec-fs-review}

Deconvolution methods choose genes in three ways:

- univariate one-versus-others screens (@sec-fs-univariate):
  differential-expression and fold-change ranks (@sec-fs-de-rank), the
  ANOVA $F$ statistic (@sec-fs-anova-rank) and specificity scores
  (@sec-gini-entropy);
- searches over the whole signature (@sec-fs-all-vs-all);
- no selection, with gene weights doing the work (@sec-fs-weighting).

This section reviews them, states where they depart from the count
model used here (@sec-fs-critiques), and compares second-generation
methods in @tbl-fs-review. Each method's likelihood is reviewed in
[5.1](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-methods).

## Univariate screens, one versus others {#sec-fs-univariate}

Classical signature pipelines score gene $g$ for type $j$ against the
remaining types, then concatenate the per-type shortlists
[@abbasDeconvolutionBloodMicroarray2009;
@newmanRobustEnumerationCell2015; @finotello_etal19].

### Differential-expression and fold-change ranks {#sec-fs-de-rank}

`limma`–voom, `edgeR` and `DESeq2` are the usual tools for
one-versus-rest contrasts [@ritchieLimmaPowersDifferential2015a;
@robinsonEdgeRBioconductorPackage2010;
@loveModeratedEstimationFold2014a]. CIBERSORT keeps genes with adjusted
$p\le0.3$, orders them by fold change and prunes the panel by its
condition number [@newmanRobustEnumerationCell2015]. Abbas et al. keep
genes whose expression in the target type exceeds that of the second-
and third-ranked types, then choose the panel with the smallest
condition number [@abbasDeconvolutionBloodMicroarray2009].
<!-- Recovered from vignettes/supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd (commit 123b937, identical in d28b91d to b0a4f2b); CIBERSORT and Abbas facts not re-checked against a local PDF. -->
On cells of one specimen these tests treat cells as replicates
(@wrn-fs-estimand); their pseudo-bulk versions need donors
(@sec-fs-cross-sample).

### ANOVA $F$ statistic {#sec-fs-anova-rank}

Wang et al. rank genes by the $F$ statistic of a type factor against an
intercept-only model [@wangSilicoEstimatesTissue2010]. This is one
omnibus test per gene instead of one test per type. Its count-model
versions, and their calibration, are the tests of tier (ii)
(@sec-fs-omnibus).

### Specificity scores {#sec-gini-entropy}

Long one-versus-rest lists are often compacted with the Shannon entropy
or the Gini coefficient of the type shares
$u_{gj}=\mu_{gj}/\sum_{\ell}\mu_{g\ell}$, as in `BioQC`
[@zhang_etal17]:

$$
H_g=-\sum_{j=1}^{J}u_{gj}\log u_{gj},
\qquad
\mathrm{Gini}_g
=
\frac{1}{2J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\lvert u_{gj}-u_{g\ell}\rvert
=
\frac1J\sum_{j=1}^{J}(2R_{gj}-J-1)\,u_{gj},
$$ {#eq-gini}

<!-- chk: V27a -->
with $0\log0=0$; $R_{gj}=R(u_{gj})$ is the rank of $u_{gj}$ among the $J$
shares of gene $g$, and $u_{g(1)}\le\cdots\le u_{g(J)}$ are its order
statistics, so that $u_{g(R_{gj})}=u_{gj}$ (rank-based notation of
Jaeckel and of Hettmansperger and McKean). $H_g/\log J$ and
$J\,\mathrm{Gini}_g/(J-1)$ lie in $[0,1]$; low entropy and high Gini mean
that few types carry the mass. @fig-gini-derivation derives the Gini
coefficient in five steps, from the mean absolute difference of the
type means to the share form of @eq-gini. The pairwise and sorted forms
agree because, the share of rank $R_{gj}$ is larger than
$R_{gj}-1$ shares and smaller than $J-R_{gj}$ shares, so it enters the
double sum with the net weight $2R_{gj}-J-1$. Both scores reward exclusive expression,
which the presence gate (@sec-fs-presence) excludes, and neither sees
redundancy between genes.

![Gini coefficient of one gene $g$ across $J=8$ cell types, from pairwise differences of the type means to the share form of @eq-gini. Left, boxes A to E: one formula per step; right, the same step for two genes with integer type means, a low-Gini gene $(12,15,9,14,11,13,10,16)$ (blue) and a high-Gini gene $(1,2,1,3,1,2,4,86)$ (orange), both with mean $\bar\mu_g=12.5$ and every $\mu_{gj}\ge1$. (D) Raw (open) and corrected (filled) coefficient, with the maximum $(J-1)/J=0.875$ (dashed) reached by a gene expressed in one type only (grey). (E) Type shares $u_{gj}$ with the line $1/J$; @eq-gini gives the same values. Code: `scripts/figures/fig_03_1_gini.R`.](figures/fig_03_1_gini.svg){#fig-gini-derivation fig-alt="Five rows joined by arrows on the left. Each row has a box with a step title, a formula and one sentence, and a chart for two genes on the right: blue for a gene with similar means in all eight types, orange for a gene with most of its counts in type 8. <!-- chk: V27b -->
For the two genes of @fig-gini-derivation the Gini coefficients are
$21/200=0.105$ and $77/100=0.770$, and the corrected values
$J\,\mathrm{Gini}_g/(J-1)$ are $3/25$ and $22/25$. A gene expressed in
one type only has $u_{g(J)}=1$, so @eq-gini gives $(J-1)/J$, the
maximum.

Concatenation does not control redundancy. Two specific markers of
different types can still be nearly collinear rows of
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ when the types share a programme (a lineage, an
activation axis), so the union of per-type lists inflates
$|\mathcal{G}|$ while $\kappa_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}})$ stays
large and NNLS or GLS fits stay unstable
[@newmanRobustEnumerationCell2015;
@avilacobosComputationalDeconvolutionTranscriptomics2018]. A criterion
on the whole signature is then needed.

## Searches over the whole signature {#sec-fs-all-vs-all}

- **Condition number.** CIBERSORT and DWLS keep the candidate signature
  with the smallest $\kappa_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}})$
  [@newmanRobustEnumerationCell2015;
  @tsoucasAccurateEstimationCelltype2019, p. 7;
  @gongDeconRNASeqStatisticalFramework2013]; its limits are in
  @sec-kappa-limits.
- **Multi-objective genetic search.** `AutoGeneS` searches gene subsets
  with a genetic algorithm that minimises the correlation between type
  centroids and maximises their distance
  [@alieeAutoGeneSAutomaticGene2021]; MOGAMUN applies the same kind of
  search to network modules
  [@novoa-del-toroMultiobjectiveGeneticAlgorithm2021]. The loss is
  defined on the full $J$-column signature, not on one-versus-rest
  lists.

Both criteria see the means only. Criteria that also use the
within-type covariance need $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$, so
they come after tier (ii) (@sec-fs-multivariate).

## Critiques of current marker rules {#sec-fs-critiques}

The reviewed marker rules (@tbl-fs-review) depart from the count model
of tier (ii) in five ways.

- **Hurdle models on droplet counts.** DWLS defines markers with the
  `MAST` hurdle model [@tsoucasAccurateEstimationCelltype2019, p. 7].
  Droplet UMI counts show no zero inflation beyond what the NB predicts
  (Svensson 2020)
  [TODO-cite: Svensson 2020, Droplet scRNA-seq is not zero-inflated, Nat. Biotechnol., doi:10.1038/s41587-019-0379-5]{.highlight},
  and current data do not support zero-inflated *measurement* models
  [@sarkarSeparatingMeasurementExpression2021, p. 5]. The hurdle splits
  one count into a detection and a magnitude test (Finak et al. 2015)
  [TODO-cite: Finak et al. 2015, MAST, Genome Biol., doi:10.1186/s13059-015-0844-5]{.highlight}
  where one NB test of @eq-fs-nb-main suffices.
- **Gaussian $t$-tests on counts.** ReDeconv uses a two-sample $t$-test
  between cells [@luTranscriptomeSizeMatters2025, p. 14]; deMixSC uses a
  paired $t$-test of bulk against matched pseudo-bulk
  [@guoDeMixSCDeconvolutionFramework2023, p. 12].
- **Cells as independent replicates.** Every test above that runs on
  cells (DWLS, ReDeconv, BayesPrism's marker option) treats them as
  replicates of a population contrast (@wrn-fs-estimand). Pseudo-bulk
  `DESeq2`, `edgeR` or `limma`–voom avoid this only with biological
  replicates at the level of the contrast (@sec-fs-cross-sample).
- **No multiplicity control.** ReDeconv keeps genes with $p<0.05$ in each
  comparison against every other type, with no FDR correction
  [@luTranscriptomeSizeMatters2025, p. 14].
- **Graph-based screens before the graph is estimated.**
  Differential-network screens (`INDEED`, D-trace) and Markov-boundary
  growth of marker seeds need fitted graphs; here they are post hoc
  (@sec-markov-seeds).

[TODO-cite: Maugé & Ventre 2026, CardamomOT, PLoS Comput. Biol. 22(10):e1014838, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014838]{.highlight}

DeCovarT builds on these methods in three ways.

- **Covariance in the criterion.** Only DeCovarT puts gene–gene
  covariance into the criterion that estimates $\boldsymbol{p}$; DECALS
  and MEAD use it only for the variance of their estimators. The other
  methods treat genes as independent, the setting in which a univariate
  screen is also the objective (@sec-fs-screen-objective). DeCovarT
  keeps the univariate screen as a gate (tier ii) and leaves the
  weighting to the covariance (tier iv).
- **One count test per gene.** The tests that select genes run on cells,
  mostly with Gaussian or hurdle models, and only DWLS (markers) and
  deMixSC (platform discrepancy) report a multiplicity correction.
  DeCovarT uses one test of the type effect per gene, chosen among four
  with known assumptions, and a Benjamini–Hochberg gate
  (@sec-fs-omnibus).
- **No perfect markers.** MuSiC and MEAD argue against marker
  pre-selection when the genes are weighted, and MEAD shows that perfect
  markers break identifiability under gene-wise platform ratios
  (@sec-fs-cross-platform); DWLS and DECALS still build marker-only
  signatures. DeCovarT removes perfect markers with the presence gate
  and weights the remaining genes.


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Tier (i): quality control and prior knowledge {#sec-fs-qc}

QC removes cells and genes that lie outside the support of any
expression model. The thresholds below are examples from the reviewed
methods (@tbl-fs-review), not defaults of DeCovarT.

- **Cells.** Library size more than 3 median absolute deviations (MAD)
  from the median of its type, and cells more than 3 MAD from the median
  pairwise distance within their type (RNA-Sieve, optional;
  @erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021, supplement p. 3).
  Fewer than 500 UMIs, fewer than 200 detected genes, or more than 50 %
  mitochondrial UMIs (deMixSC; @guoDeMixSCDeconvolutionFramework2023,
  p. 11).
- **Genes.** Ribosomal, mitochondrial and sex-chromosome genes, which
  reflect cell survival and donor sex rather than type
  (BayesPrism; @chuCellTypeGeneExpression2022, supplement pp. 14, 19).
  Genes detected in fewer than 20 % of the cells of every type
  (RNA-Sieve, supplement p. 3).

## Prior-knowledge markers {#sec-fs-prior-markers}

A short curated list of markers (lineage or signalling genes named by
the biology of the tissue) enters as hard prior knowledge. These genes
are kept whatever their rank in tier (ii), provided they pass the
presence gate, and they are reported as a separate group. Two rules
keep the list honest. It is fixed before the data-driven ranks are
seen. It is never used to score the data-driven panel, since a panel
judged by its overlap with the markers that were forced into it is
judged by construction. The overlap between the curated list and the
genes that the data-driven tiers keep can be reported as a description,
for example with a hypergeometric tail, as the reproducibility book
does.

## Presence gate in every type {#sec-fs-presence}

::: callout-note
## Necessary, not sufficient

A gene enters tier (ii) only if

$$
\min_{j}\delta_{gj}\ge\delta_{\min}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\min_{j}v_{gj}>0,
$$ {#eq-fs-presence}

with $\delta_{\min}$ a few per cent (for example $0.05$), fixed before
the ranks are seen. [These are necessary conditions for a non-singular
within-type covariance and for an identifiable $\boldsymbol{p}$; they
are not sufficient.]{.mark} Two cases show what the gate excludes.

<!-- chk: V17a, V17b -->
- **Zero in every cell of type $j$.** Then $v_{gj}=0$ and the whole row
  and column $g$ of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ are zero: $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ is
  singular ($\det\boldsymbol{V}_j=0$), the correlation
  $v_{gh}/\sqrt{v_{gg}v_{hh}}$ is $0/0$ and so undefined, and the fitted
  type-$j$ Gaussian is degenerate, a point mass in coordinate $g$. Its
  likelihood is unbounded, so no maximum-likelihood estimate exists.
- **Detected in a single cell $c$.** With count $a$ in that cell, the
  centred counts of $g$ are $a(\boldsymbol{e}_c-\mathbf{1}/C_j)$, and
  its correlation with any gene $h$ is
  $r_{gh}=\tilde h_c/(\sqrt{1-1/C_j}\,\lVert\tilde{\boldsymbol h}\rVert)$,
  $\tilde{\boldsymbol h}$ the centred counts of $h$: one cell sets it.
  Two genes detected only in cell $c$ have $r=1$ whatever their counts,
  a perfect and degenerate correlation, and $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ is again
  singular.

<!-- chk: V17c, V10a, V10c -->
With $\delta_{\min}C_j\ge2$ the gate keeps only genes with at least two
non-zero cells in every type, which excludes both cases. It does not
make $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ invertible: $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{V}_j\le
\min(C_j-1,G)$, so $\boldsymbol{V}_j$ is singular whenever $G\ge C_j$ or
genes satisfy an exact linear relation, and shrinkage is still needed
([3.2](03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html)). Nor does it make
$\boldsymbol{p}$ identifiable, which requires a non-singular Fisher
information for $\boldsymbol{p}$
([1.2](01-2-population-inference.html#sec-identifiability)). The gate
also removes perfect markers, whose effect under gene-wise platform
ratios is in @sec-fs-cross-platform.
:::


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Tier (ii): cross-cell consistency {#sec-fs-consistency}

MuSiC introduced "marker gene consistency" with two parts
[@wangBulkTissueCell2019, p. 2].
[Cross-cell consistency asks whether a gene is stable across the cells
of one type]{.mark}, so that biased cell capture does not drive its
selection; cross-cell consistent genes have a low within-cluster
variance [@wangBulkTissueCell2019, p. 3].
[Cross-sample consistency asks whether a gene's type mean is stable
across specimens]{.mark} (MuSiC's cross-subject consistency), and needs
at least two of them. With a reference from one specimen only cross-cell
consistency can be assessed from the reference alone; cross-sample
consistency is a perspective (@sec-fs-cross-sample), and consistency
with a matched bulk is tier (iii) (@sec-fs-cross-platform). The natural
statistic for cross-cell consistency splits a gene's variation into
between-type and within-type parts.

## Count null model and Pearson residuals {#sec-sctransform}

The technical null fits each gene with library size as the only
covariate,

$$
M_{0}:\;
\log m_{gc}=\beta_{0g}+\log s_{c},
\qquad
x_{gc}\sim\mathrm{NB}(m_{gc},\psi_{g}),
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(x_{gc})=V(m_{gc})=m_{gc}+\frac{m_{gc}^{2}}{\psi_g}.
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-null}

$M_0$ is fitted gene by gene with our own NB
GLM, with $\psi_g$ estimated per gene by maximum likelihood (for
example with `glmGamPoi` [@glmGamPoi2020] or `MASS::glm.nb()`), and its
residuals are not clipped^[`SCTransform` with `vst.flavor = "v2"` fits
the same model, with the depth slope fixed and library size as an
offset, but it regularises $\psi_g$ across genes and clips the residuals
at $\pm\sqrt{C/30}$ [@hafemeisterNormalizationVarianceStabilization2019;
@lauseAnalyticPearsonResiduals2021]. Clipping is harmful
for gene selection: it shrinks exactly the cells with large residuals
and large fitted means, which include the informative high-leverage
cells of a rare type and of highly expressed genes, such as
haemoglobins or master regulators (@sec-fs-leverage).]

The raw Pearson residual is

$$
r_{gc}=\frac{x_{gc}-\hat m_{gc}}{\sqrt{V(\hat m_{gc})}},
\qquad
r^{\mathrm{SP}}_{gc}=\frac{r_{gc}}{\sqrt{\hat\phi_g\,(1-h_{gc})}},
$$ {#eq-fs-pearson}

and $r^{\mathrm{SP}}_{gc}$ is the standardised Pearson residual
[@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. $\hat\phi_g$ is the Pearson
dispersion (the sum of squared $r_{gc}$ divided by the residual degrees
of freedom), and $h_{gc}$ the leverage of cell $c$ in the weighted hat
matrix of the final IRLS step. The factor $1-h_{gc}$ corrects for a
fitted value that a high-leverage cell partly sets itself.
`SCTransform` residuals are raw residuals: they carry neither
$\hat\phi_g$ nor $1-h_{gc}$, and they are clipped. Standardised does
not mean Gaussian: at low means Pearson residuals stay discrete and
skewed, and randomised quantile residuals (Dunn & Smyth 1996)
[TODO-cite: Dunn & Smyth 1996, Randomized quantile residuals, J. Comput. Graph. Stat. 5(3):236-244, doi:10.1080/10618600.1996.10474708]{.highlight}
are the residuals to compare with a normal reference.

The raw residuals of $M_0$ split as

$$
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{B},g}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}C_{j}\bigl(\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}\bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{W},g}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{c:j(c)=j}\bigl(r_{gc}-\bar r_{gj}\bigr)^{2},
$$ {#eq-fs-ss}

with $\bar r_{gj}$ the mean residual in type $j$ and $\bar r_{g}$ the
overall mean ($\approx0$). A lineage marker has a large between-type and
a small within-type part; a stress-response gene can have a large total
residual variance and still a small between-type part. The sums weight
every cell equally, so the abundant types dominate them; tests that
allow a different variance per type are in @sec-fs-calibration.
@fig-sc-transform shows the steps of the null model on simulated
counts.

![Count null model $M_0$ on simulated counts (2,000 genes, 2,000 cells of two types, seed 20261101), drawn with the `SCTransform` (v2) workflow. (a) Gene variance against gene mean: NB variance with the smoothed dispersion (solid) and the Poisson line (dashed). (b) Counts of one marker gene against the size factor, with the fitted mean of $M_0$ (library size as offset, no cell type). (c) Per-gene dispersion estimates against the gene mean, which $M_0$ uses here, and their smooth across genes, the empirical-Bayes regularisation that `SCTransform` uses instead. (d) Raw Pearson residuals of the same gene: no trend with depth, the type difference kept. Code: `scripts/figures/fig_03_1_sctransform.R`.](figures/fig_03_1_sctransform.svg){#fig-sc-transform fig-alt="Four scatter panels joined by arrows and labelled with formulas. Panel a: gene variance against gene mean on log scales, points above the Poisson line and close to the negative-binomial curve. Panel b: counts of one gene against the size factor for two cell types, with the fitted mean rising in proportion to the size factor. Panel c: per-gene dispersion estimates against the mean, scattered around an increasing smooth curve. Panel d: Pearson residuals of the same gene against the size factor, centred on zero with no depth trend, the two cell types at different levels."}

## Four tests of the type effect {#sec-fs-omnibus}

Add the type main effect to @eq-fs-nb-null:

$$
M_{1}:\;
\log m_{gc}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_{g,j(c)}+\log s_{c},
\qquad
\beta_{g1}=0,
\qquad
H_{0g}:\beta_{g2}=\cdots=\beta_{gJ}=0 .
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-main}

The joint null has $J-1$ degrees of freedom
[@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. One omnibus test per gene
replaces $\binom{J}{2}$ pairwise or $J$ one-versus-rest tests, and a
single Benjamini–Hochberg correction across genes follows. Four tests
of $H_{0g}$ are compared (@tbl-fs-tests). The presence gate removes the
all-zero types near which the Wald test fails (Hauck–Donner effect;
@yeeHauckDonnerEffectWald2022), so the Wald test is not used.

- **Likelihood ratio (analysis of deviance).**
  $\Lambda_g=\mathcal{D}_g(M_0)-\mathcal{D}_g(M_1)$, with both models
  fitted at the $\hat\psi_g$ of $M_1$, referred to $\chi^2_{J-1}$. It
  needs one $M_1$ fit per gene, a one-way GLM with $J$ coefficients.
- **One-way ANOVA $F$ on variance-stabilised counts.** The shifted
  logarithm $\log(x_{gc}/s_c+y_0)$, with $y_0=\psi_0/4$ for a typical
  dispersion $\psi_0$, stabilises the NB variance and performs as well
  as more elaborate transformations in a published benchmark
  (Ahlmann-Eltze & Huber 2023)
  [TODO-cite: Ahlmann-Eltze & Huber 2023, Comparison of transformations for single-cell RNA-seq data, Nat. Methods 20, doi:10.1038/s41592-023-01814-1]{.highlight}.
  The $F$ statistic of the type factor on these values is referred to
  $F_{J-1,C-J}$ [@wangSilicoEstimatesTissue2010]. When the variance on
  the transformed scale still differs between types, Welch's
  heteroscedastic one-way test (Welch 1951)
  [TODO-cite: Welch 1951, On the comparison of several mean values: an alternative approach, Biometrika 38:330-336]{.highlight}
  is the fallback.
- **Quasi-likelihood $F$.** Defined below (@eq-fs-qlf).
- **Permutation calibration.** Welch's statistic on the residuals of
  $M_0$, referred to a permutation distribution (@sec-fs-calibration).

**Quasi-likelihood $F$.** Dividing $\Lambda_g/(J-1)$ by the Pearson
dispersion of $M_1$ gives

$$
F_{g}
=
\frac{\Lambda_g/(J-1)}{\hat\phi_g},
\qquad
\hat\phi_g=\frac{1}{C-J}\sum_{c}\frac{(x_{gc}-\hat m^{(1)}_{gc})^{2}}{V(\hat m^{(1)}_{gc})},
$$ {#eq-fs-qlf}

with $\hat m^{(1)}_{gc}$ the fitted means of $M_1$, referred to
$F_{J-1,C-J}$. The mean model @eq-fs-nb-main and the variance function
$V(m)=m+m^2/\psi_g$ are kept, and a scalar $\phi_g$ absorbs a variance
larger or smaller than $V$ predicts. This is the quasi-likelihood $F$
test of the edgeR pipeline and of `glmGamPoi::test_de()`, which use the
deviance in the numerator and also shrink $\hat\phi_g$ across genes
[@lundDetectingDifferentialExpression2012; @glmGamPoi2020]. Three
consequences follow.

- **Keep overdispersed genes.** Within-type overdispersion is the
  within-type scatter that the denominator already penalises, and the
  covariance that DeCovarT models. Removing such genes before the test
  removes that signal.
- **A scalar $\phi_g$ cannot absorb a wrong variance function.** Under a
  Poisson null it cannot absorb the quadratic NB term, whose share grows
  with the type mean; the pooled $\hat\phi_g$ is then wrong for every
  type. Use the NB variance, so that $\phi_g\approx1$ in every type. If
  the dispersion still differs between types, $\hat\phi_g$ is an average
  dominated by the large types, and a statistic with one variance per
  type, Welch's $G$ referred to permutations, is needed
  (@sec-fs-calibration).
- **Gate, then rank by effect size.** $F_g$ grows with the counts of a
  gene as well as with its effect, so it serves as a gate, not as a
  rank. Genes that pass the FDR gate are ranked by an effect size, the
  deviance explained $R^{2}_{D,g}=1-\mathcal{D}_g(M_1)/\mathcal{D}_g(M_0)$
  or the ratio $\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{B},g}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{W},g}$
  of @eq-fs-ss, not by $p$-value.

| Test | Statistic | Reference law | Assumptions | R function |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Analysis of deviance (LR) | $\Lambda_g=\mathcal{D}_g(M_0)-\mathcal{D}_g(M_1)$ | $\chi^2_{J-1}$ | NB mean and variance correct; $\psi_g$ treated as known; enough counts per type | `MASS::glm.nb()` for both models, `stats::pchisq()` |
| One-way ANOVA $F$ on the shifted logarithm | between/within mean squares of $\log(x_{gc}/s_c+y_0)$ | $F_{J-1,C-J}$ | equal variance across types on the transformed scale; approximately normal type means | `stats::oneway.test(var.equal = TRUE)`; Welch: `var.equal = FALSE` |
| Quasi-likelihood $F$ | @eq-fs-qlf | $F_{J-1,C-J}$ | NB mean model and variance function up to one scalar $\phi_g$ for all types | `glmGamPoi::test_de()`, `edgeR::glmQLFTest()` |
| Permuted Welch $G$ | Welch's $G$ on the Pearson residuals of $M_0$ | permutation distribution, $B$ label permutations shared by all genes | labels fixed in advance; residuals of $M_0$ exchangeable across cells under $H_{0g}$; type-specific variances allowed | `permuco::aovperm()` (Freedman–Lane, linear models, permutes $F$); `flipscores::flipscores()` (GLMs) |

: Four tests of the type effect for one gene. $C$ is the number of cells and $J$ the number of types. {#tbl-fs-tests}

When the NB variance function itself fails, quasi-likelihood with an
empirical variance function is the fallback
[@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. When the *shape* differs
between types (types that share a mean but differ in dispersion), a
location–scale model with type-specific $\psi_{gj}$ tests both, on
$2(J-1)$ degrees of freedom; this is the GAMLSS margin used by scDesign3
[@songScDesign3GeneratesRealistic2024], Stasinopoulos & Rigby (2007)
[TODO-cite: Stasinopoulos & Rigby 2007, GAMLSS in R, J. Stat. Softw. 23(7), doi:10.18637/jss.v023.i07]{.highlight}.
Whether a dispersion difference should count as a type effect depends
on the use: for a gate on mean effects it is a false discovery, while
for DeCovarT, which models the within-type covariance, such a gene can
still carry information.

### Permutation calibration {#sec-fs-calibration}

A permutation null keeps a statistic and replaces its reference
distribution by the distribution under random relabelling of the
cells.

- **Freedman–Lane.** With nuisance covariates (batch, cell line, cell
  cycle), a global label shuffle creates impossible combinations. The
  Freedman–Lane scheme fits the reduced model without type, permutes its
  residuals, adds them back to the reduced fit, refits the full model
  and recomputes the statistic
  [@freedmanNonstochasticInterpretation1983]. In a comparison of
  permutation strategies for the general linear model, Winkler et al.
  (2014) write "we recommend the Freedman–Lane and the Smith methods"
  (p. 393)
  [TODO-cite: Winkler, Ridgway, Webster, Smith & Nichols 2014, Permutation inference for the general linear model, NeuroImage 92:381-397, doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.01.060]{.highlight}.
  Here the nuisance part of $M_0$ is an intercept and the depth
  offset, so the reduced residuals are the label-free Pearson residuals
  of $M_0$, and Freedman–Lane reduces to permuting the labels against
  them.
- **Welch's $G$, not $F$.** Welch's statistic weights each type mean by
  $C_j$ over its own within-type variance and corrects the denominator
  for the estimated variances (Winkler et al. 2014, Eqs 6–7). With one
  variance group $G=F$. Under heteroscedasticity $F$ is not pivotal
  (p. 386): its null distribution then depends on the unknown
  type-specific variances, and a label permutation does not reproduce
  them. $G$ stays approximately pivotal, so its permutation $p$-value
  remains close to its nominal level.
- **One permutation for all genes.** The same $B$ permutations of the
  cell labels are applied to every gene. Each gene keeps its marginal
  distribution and its dependence on the other genes; only the link with
  the label is broken. Shuffling genes, or shuffling within cells, does
  not produce that null.
- **Smallest $p$-value.** With
  $p_g=(1+\#\{G^{*}_g\ge G_g\})/(B+1)$, the smallest attainable value
  is $1/(B+1)$. For smaller $p$-values, a generalised Pareto fit to the
  upper tail of the permutation distribution gives an approximation
  (Knijnenburg et al. 2009; Winkler et al. 2016)
  [TODO-cite: Knijnenburg, Wessels, Reinders & Shmulevich 2009, Fewer permutations, more accurate P-values, Bioinformatics 25(12):i161-i168, doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btp211]{.highlight}
  [TODO-cite: Winkler, Ridgway, Douaud, Nichols & Smith 2016, Faster permutation inference in brain imaging, NeuroImage 141:502-516, doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2016.05.068]{.highlight}.

`permuco` implements Freedman–Lane for linear models and ANOVA
(Frossard & Renaud 2021)
[TODO-cite: Frossard & Renaud 2021, Permutation tests for regression, ANOVA, and comparison of signals: the permuco package, J. Stat. Softw. 99(15), doi:10.18637/jss.v099.i15]{.highlight}.
For GLMs, `flipscores` flips the signs of the score contributions
instead of permuting, and stays valid when the variance is
misspecified (Hemerik, Goeman & Finos 2020; De Santis et al. 2025)
[TODO-cite: Hemerik, Goeman & Finos 2020, Robust testing in generalized linear models by sign flipping score contributions, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 82(3), doi:10.1111/rssb.12369]{.highlight}
[TODO-cite: De Santis et al. 2025, J. Am. Stat. Assoc., doi:10.1080/01621459.2025.2491775]{.highlight}.
Neither package computes Welch's $G$; the figure script below permutes
it directly. PERMANOVA is the multivariate sum-of-squares version of the
same permutation test (Anderson 2001; `vegan::adonis2()`)
[TODO-cite: Anderson 2001, A new method for non-parametric multivariate analysis of variance, Austral Ecol. 26(1):32-46, doi:10.1111/j.1442-9993.2001.01070.pp.x]{.highlight};
a module-level version is a perspective (@sec-fs-multivariate-tests).

### The four tests on simulated counts {#sec-fs-tests-simulation}

The tests rank genes by the same type effect, so their gene orders
should agree; @fig-fs-type-tests measures how far they do. The
simulation has $J=4$ types of 2,000, 300, 60 and 25 cells and 1,000
genes: 600 nulls with one dispersion per gene, 300 nulls with the same
mean in every type but $\psi_{gj}=20$ in the two large types and $1$ in
the two small ones, and 100 genes with a type effect.

- **Gene order.** Over all genes, Kendall's $\tau_b$ is 0.98 between the
  LR and QL $F$ rankings, 0.67 between LR and ANOVA, and 0.73 between LR
  and the permuted Welch $G$. Among the 100 alternatives, LR and ANOVA
  agree more (0.90) and the permuted $G$ less (0.53 to 0.58).
- **Type I error.** Under the homoscedastic null all tests reject at
  most 4.8 % of the genes at 0.05. Under type-specific dispersion, LR,
  QL $F$ and ANOVA reject 15 % to 19 % of the nulls, and the permuted
  $F$ on the same residuals 18 %; the permuted $G$ rejects 6 %. QL $F$
  behaves like LR because the median $\hat\phi_g$ is 0.999 in both
  nulls: the pooled dispersion is set by the 2,300 cells of the large
  types.
- **Power.** The permuted $G$ pays for its calibration. With
  Benjamini–Hochberg at 0.05 it makes 43 discoveries, with an empirical
  FDR of 0.05 and a power of 0.41; LR makes 105, with an FDR of 0.19 and
  a power of 0.85. 35 of the 100 alternatives reach the permutation
  floor $1/(B+1)$ with $B=2{,}000$, where the generalised Pareto tail
  would separate them. Welch's $G$ referred to its analytic
  $F$ approximation instead of permutations (not drawn) rejects 11 % of
  the homoscedastic nulls; the skewness of the residuals of the
  25-cell type is a likely cause (not checked).

The trade-off is between a gate that is calibrated when dispersion
differs between types (permuted $G$) and a gate with more power when
the NB variance function holds (LR, QL $F$). Under type-specific
dispersion the GAMLSS test above answers a different question, a change
in the count law rather than in its mean.


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Tier (iii): cross-platform consistency {#sec-fs-cross-platform}

A gene can be a perfect cross-cell marker and still be measured
differently by the reference and the bulk protocol. Cross-platform
consistency compares the bulk with the single-cell reference, and
needs a bulk sample that matches the reference (same tissue, ideally
the same specimen). The reviewed methods handle it in four ways.

- **Range bound (RNA-Sieve).** Per cell, the expected bulk is a convex
  combination of the type means, so on a common scale

  $$
  \min_{j}\tilde\mu_{gj}\;\le\;\operatorname{E}\tilde y_{g}\;\le\;\max_{j}\tilde\mu_{gj}.
  $$ {#eq-fs-range}

  RNA-Sieve removes genes whose bulk value falls outside this range by
  more than a sub-Gaussian tail allows (@sec-fs-range-tail), and genes
  that are MAD outliers on four summary statistics (largest type mean,
  largest type standard deviation, largest coefficient of variation,
  and a bulk-to-reference ratio)
  [@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021, p. 11, Eqs.
  12–13]. The bound holds for any weights on the simplex, so it does not
  depend on whether $\boldsymbol{p}$ or $\boldsymbol{q}$ is the target.
  A gene-wise platform ratio $\tilde b_g$ far from 1 moves the bulk
  outside the range; the filter detects that case.
- **Test against a matched benchmark (deMixSC).** A paired $t$-test of
  real bulk against pseudo-bulk of the same aliquots, with BH at 0.05;
  the discrepant genes are kept and down-weighted by a fixed factor of
  1,000 [@guoDeMixSCDeconvolutionFramework2023, p. 12].
- **Gene-wise platform ratios in the model.** MEAD lets the ratios vary
  by gene with mean 1 [@xieStatisticalInferenceCell2026, pp. 5, 8]; RCTD
  uses a gene-wise platform random effect, estimated once from a pooled
  pseudo-bulk and then fixed [@cableRobustDecompositionCell2022a,
  pp. 3, 6–7]; MuSiC allows a gene- and subject-specific intercept
  [@wangBulkTissueCell2019, p. 7].
- **Normalisation only.** ReDeconv applies gene-length normalisation to
  the bulk only [@luTranscriptomeSizeMatters2025, p. 2].

Gene-wise ratios have a price. MEAD shows that the proportions are not
identifiable when all genes are perfect markers and gene-wise ratios
are allowed: rescaling the ratios of the markers of type $j$ by a
common factor is absorbed by the proportions
[@xieStatisticalInferenceCell2026, p. 7]. The presence gate
(@sec-fs-presence) excludes these genes. Modelling a gene-wise or
module-wise scale $\tilde b_g$ inside DeCovarT is a perspective of
[5.3](05-3-extensions-roadmap.html).

DeCovarT's tier (iii) has two parts: influence diagnostics for cells
and genes (@sec-fs-leverage), and a bulk filter whose thresholds come
from tail statements for a discrepancy between the bulk and the
reference (@sec-fs-range-tail).

## Outlier cells and genes: leverage and influence {#sec-fs-leverage}

Residual size, leverage and influence are three different quantities
[@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. Leverage measures how
unusual an observation is in the design, the residual how badly the
model predicts its response, and influence how much the fit changes
when the observation is removed. Influence needs both.

| | Large standardised residual | Small standardised residual |
|---|---|---|
| **High leverage** | potentially influential: inspect | extreme design point, often benign |
| **Low leverage** | response outlier, limited influence | ordinary observation |

: Leverage and residual size combine into influence. {#tbl-fs-leverage-residual}

**Cells.** In the gene-wise GLM $M_1$ of @eq-fs-nb-main, leverage
belongs to the cells, not to the gene. For a one-way design with a log
link the hat value of cell $c$ is

$$
h_{gc}=\frac{w_{gc}}{\sum_{c':\,j(c')=j(c)}w_{gc'}},
\qquad
w_{gc}=\frac{\hat m_{gc}^{2}}{V(\hat m_{gc})},
\qquad
\mathrm{Cook}_{gc}
=
\frac{(r^{\mathrm{SP}}_{gc})^{2}}{J}\,\frac{h_{gc}}{1-h_{gc}}
=
\frac{r_{gc}^{2}\,h_{gc}}{J\,\hat\phi_g\,(1-h_{gc})^{2}},
$$ {#eq-fs-cook-cells}

<!-- chk: V28a, V28b -->
with $w_{gc}$ the IRLS weight. The hat values of each type sum to 1,
so a cell of a type with $C_j$ cells has $h_{gc}\approx1/C_j$, and
within a type $h_{gc}$ grows with the fitted mean. Every cell of a rare
type, and every cell with a large fitted mean, has high leverage.
@fig-fs-influence-cells shows the consequence. The 25 cells of the rare
high-expression type have leverage near 0.04; the 23 consistent ones
have small residuals and a Cook's distance of at most 0.025. Two
doublet-like cells of that type combine that leverage with a residual
near 6 and have the largest Cook's distances, 0.36 and 0.34. Three
outliers of the 2,000-cell type have larger residuals, 6.1 to 7.3, but
a leverage below $10^{-3}$, and their Cook's distances stay below 0.01.
No cell passes the conventional cut of 0.5, and the cut $4/C$ flags 12
of the 23 consistent rare-type cells on leverage alone.

Colours: type 1 grey, type 2 green, type 3 blue, type 4 (rare, high-expression marker) orange. Triangles D1 and D2: doublet-like type-4 cells with counts four times their fitted mean; squares O1–O3: type-1 cells with counts eight times theirs. (a) Randomised quantile residual (Dunn & Smyth 1996) against the fitted mean $\hat m_{gc}$ (log scale); dotted lines at $\pm3$. (b) Normal QQ plot of the randomised quantile residuals, with the line $y=x$. (d) Cook's distance against $h/(1-h)$, both on log scales; dotted lines of equal $|r^{\mathrm{SP}}|$ (1, 2, 3, 6); dashed line at $4/C$; values below $10^{-6}$ are drawn on the lower edge. Panel c: standardised Pearson residual against leverage on a log scale; each type forms its own band, from leverage near 0.0005 for the largest type to near 0.04 for the rare type; the two rare-type doublets sit at high leverage with residuals near 6, just inside the dashed Cook 0.5 contour, while three large-type outliers have residuals of 6 to 7 at leverage below 0.001, far from the contours. Panel d: Cook's distance against leverage ratio on log-log axes with dotted lines of equal residual; the doublets and the large-type outliers lie near the same residual line of 6, and the doublets have a Cook's distance 40 to 80 times larger."}

**Genes.** At the level of the bulk, the observations are genes:
regress the bulk per cell $\tilde y_{gi}$ on the reference signature,
the row $\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}}_{g\cdot}$, by weighted least
squares with weights $1/\tau_g^{2}$, $\tau_g^{2}$ the variance of the
bulk residual of gene $g$. With $\boldsymbol{X}$ the $G\times J$ matrix
of reference means and $\boldsymbol{W}=\operatorname{diag}(1/\tau_g^{2})$,

$$
h_g=\frac{\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}}_{g\cdot}^{\top}\bigl(\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{X}\bigr)^{-1}\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}}_{g\cdot}}{\tau_g^{2}},
\qquad
\mathrm{Cook}_g=\frac{r_g^{2}}{J}\,\frac{h_g}{1-h_g},
$$ {#eq-fs-hat-genes}

<!-- chk: V28c -->
with $r_g$ the standardised residual of gene $g$. $h_g$ depends on the
scaled row $\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}}_{g\cdot}/\tau_g$. When
$\tau_g$ grows in proportion to the level of the gene, the level
cancels and the leverage follows the direction of the gene's profile
across types, not its level. In @fig-fs-influence-genes the markers of
the rarest type and a high-mean gene with a rare-type profile have the
highest leverage, 0.024 to 0.044. A gene with a mean 50 times the
median and an ordinary profile has a leverage of 0.017, against 0.70 in
an unweighted fit. All of these genes have small residuals and a Cook's
distance below 0.021. The ten platform-discordant genes
($\tilde b_g=4$) have residuals of 2.9 to 10.3; the largest Cook's
distances, 0.48 and 0.33, combine a residual near 10 with a leverage
near 0.02. The discordant genes also inflate the residual variance of
the fit, from 0.96 to 3.35, which shrinks every standardised residual.

Two rules follow from @tbl-fs-leverage-residual and the two figures.
[A cell or a gene is flagged only when both its leverage and its
standardised residual are large]{.mark}; neither a fixed Cook cut (0.5
or 1 flags nothing in either figure) nor $4/C$ or $4/G$ alone separates
the injected outliers from consistent high-leverage observations. Rules
that shrink by size alone, such as residual clipping or SCDC's clipping
of variance weights at the 15th and 85th percentiles
[@dongSCDCBulkGene2021, p. 10], shrink the informative high-leverage
observations together with the harmful ones.

## Bulk consistency filter {#sec-fs-range-tail}

Two statistics compare one bulk sample $i$ with the reference. The
first does not need the composition. RNA-Sieve writes its range filter
as a probability [@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021,
Eq. 12, PDF p. 11, Genome Res. p. 1804]:

$$
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t\bigr),
\qquad
\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g
=\inf\Bigl\{\lvert\tilde y_{gi}-a\rvert:\ \min_{j}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\le a\le\max_{j}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\Bigr\},
$$ {#eq-fs-rnasieve-12}

the distance of the bulk per cell to the range of the reference means.
The paper states only that this probability "decays in $t$ with
sub-Gaussian tails", with constants that depend on the type variances,
and that computing "the precise tail bounds" requires the true
composition; it prints no constant. The second statistic uses a
composition $\hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i}$ and the scale $a_i$:

$$
D_{gi}=\frac{\tilde y_{gi}}{a_i}-\sum_{j=1}^{J}\hat p_{ji}\,\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj},
\qquad
S_M=\sum_{g\in M}\frac{D_{gi}}{\operatorname{sd}D_{gi}},
$$ {#eq-fs-discrepancy}

with $S_M$ its standardised sum over a gene module $M$. Under a
consistent platform $D_{gi}$ is centred at 0; a gene-wise ratio
$\tilde b_g\neq1$ shifts it by $(\tilde b_g-1)\sum_jp_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}$;
@sec-fs-platform-ratio divides a plug-in ratio out of the bulk before
$D_{gi}$ is formed.
A gene is flagged when $\lvert D_{gi}\rvert$ exceeds a threshold
$t_{\alpha}$ that a consistent gene exceeds with probability at most
$\alpha$. The thresholds come from concentration inequalities, recalled
without proof in three notes, and from five tail statements
(@sec-fs-five-bounds).

::: {#nte-fs-subexp .callout-note}
## Sub-exponential variables

Vershynin's Proposition 2.8.1 (2nd ed., p. 44) states that, for a
random variable $X$, the following properties are equivalent, with
parameters $\eta_i>0$ that differ by at most an absolute constant
factor
[TODO-cite: Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press]{.highlight}:

- **(i) Tails.** $\mathbb{P}\{\lvert X\rvert\ge t\}\le2\exp(-t/\eta_1)$
  for all $t\ge0$.
- **(ii) Moments.**
  $(\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert^{\nu})^{1/\nu}\le\eta_2\,\nu$ for
  every moment order $\nu\ge1$.
- **(iii) MGF of $\lvert X\rvert$.**
  $\operatorname{E}\exp(\lvert X\rvert/\eta_3)\le2$.
- **(iv) MGF.** If $\operatorname{E}X=0$, (i)–(iii) are also equivalent
  to $\operatorname{E}\exp(uX)\le\exp(\eta_4^{2}u^{2})$ for all
  $\lvert u\rvert\le1/\eta_4$.

<!-- chk: V20b -->
Property $i$ implies property $j$ with $\eta_j\le\gamma'\eta_i$ for an
absolute constant $\gamma'$ (footnote 7). The sub-exponential norm is
the smallest $\eta_3$ in (iii) (Definition 2.8.4, Eq. 2.25, p. 45):

$$
\lVert X\rVert_{\psi_1}=\inf\bigl\{\eta>0:\ \operatorname{E}\exp(\lvert X\rvert/\eta)\le2\bigr\}.
$$ {#eq-fs-psi1}

Centring costs an absolute constant,
$\lVert X-\operatorname{E}X\rVert_{\psi_1}\le\gamma'\lVert X\rVert_{\psi_1}$
(Eq. 2.26, p. 46). Bounded variables are sub-Gaussian, and sub-Gaussian
variables are sub-exponential (Remark 2.8.8, p. 46). A product of two
sub-Gaussian variables is sub-exponential (Lemma 2.8.6), so sample
variances and covariances, the inputs of
[3.2](03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html), concentrate as
Bernstein's inequality describes, not Hoeffding's (our remark).

**NB counts.** Let $X$ follow an NB law with mean $m$ and size $\psi$,
$\mathbb{P}(X=x)=\binom{x+\psi-1}{x}\pi^{x}(1-\pi)^{\psi}$ for
$x\in\{0,1,\dots\}$, $\pi=m/(m+\psi)$ and variance $m+m^{2}/\psi$ (the
law of @eq-fs-nb-null with $m=m_{gc}$, $\psi=\psi_g$). Its moment
generating function is (our derivation)

$$
M(u)
=\operatorname{E}e^{uX}
=\Bigl(\frac{1-\pi}{1-\pi e^{u}}\Bigr)^{\psi},
\qquad
u<-\log\pi ,
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-mgf}

<!-- chk: V20a -->
and it is infinite for $u\ge-\log\pi$. Finite in an open interval
around 0, it gives property (iii) for the centred NB, which is
therefore sub-exponential (our derivation). It is not sub-Gaussian: a
sub-Gaussian variable has a finite moment generating function at every
$u$, and @eq-fs-nb-mgf diverges at $-\log\pi$. On the log scale the
tail $\mathbb{P}(X\ge x)$ is linear in $x$, not quadratic. Vershynin's
list of sub-exponential laws contains the Poisson and the geometric but
not the NB (Example 2.8.7, p. 46). For an integer $\psi$ the NB is a sum
of $\psi$ geometric variables; @eq-fs-nb-mgf covers every $\psi>0$.
:::

::: {#nte-fs-hoeffding .callout-note}
## Hoeffding's inequality

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent, and let $X_\nu$ take its values in
an interval of length $A_\nu$. Then, for every $t>0$,
$\mathbb{P}\{\sum_{\nu}(X_\nu-\operatorname{E}X_\nu)\ge t\}\le\exp(-2t^{2}/\sum_{\nu}A_\nu^{2})$,
and the same bound holds for the lower tail (Vershynin, Theorem 2.2.6,
p. 30; Mohri, Rostamizadeh & Talwalkar 2012, Theorem D.1, p. 370)
[TODO-cite: Mohri, Rostamizadeh & Talwalkar 2012, Foundations of Machine Learning, MIT Press, Appendix D (book pp. 369-378)]{.highlight}.
The variables must be bounded and independent. The bound uses the
ranges, not the variances.
:::

RNA-Sieve's likelihood rests on "the classical CLT ... as long as
$\operatorname{Var}(\nu_{g,k})<\infty$, which is true because gene
expression profiles are necessarily bounded" (PDF p. 10, Genome Res.
p. 1803). A central limit theorem gives no tail bound at finite sample
size; the sub-Gaussian claim follows from boundedness. With the
expression of gene $g$ in one cell in $[0,A_g]$, Hoeffding's inequality
for the means of the $n_i$ bulk cells and of the $C_j$ reference cells,
and a union bound, give (our derivation)

$$
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t\bigr)
\;\le\;
2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{n_i\,t^2}{2A_g^2}\Bigr)
+2\sum_{j=1}^{J}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{C_j\,t^2}{2A_g^2}\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-fs-range-tail}

<!-- chk: V19a, V19b, V19c -->
because the expected bulk lies in the range of the expected type means
(@eq-fs-range), so $\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t$ requires a deviation of
at least $t/2$ of the bulk mean or of one reference mean. Like the
paper's model, the bound treats the bulk as $n_i$ independent cells; it
is conservative. Counts have no bound $A_g$.

::: {#nte-fs-bernstein .callout-note}
## Bernstein's inequality

**Sub-exponential form** (Vershynin, Theorem 2.9.1, p. 47). Let
$X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent, mean-zero, sub-exponential. Then, for
every $t\ge0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl\{\Bigl\lvert\sum_{\nu=1}^{n}X_\nu\Bigr\rvert\ge t\Bigr\}
\le
2\exp\Bigl[-\gamma\min\Bigl(\frac{t^{2}}{\sum_{\nu}\lVert X_\nu\rVert_{\psi_1}^{2}},\ \frac{t}{\max_\nu\lVert X_\nu\rVert_{\psi_1}}\Bigr)\Bigr],
$$ {#eq-fs-bernstein}

where $\gamma>0$ is an absolute constant that the theorem does not
give. The bound "has *two tails* – gaussian and exponential"
(Remark 2.9.3, p. 48): Gaussian for small deviations and exponential
for large ones, where a single dominant term drives the tail
(Remark 2.9.4, p. 48).

**Bounded form, explicit constants** (Vershynin, Theorem 2.9.5, p. 49).
If moreover $\lvert X_\nu\rvert\le A$ for all $\nu$, then
$\mathbb{P}\{\lvert\sum_\nu X_\nu\rvert\ge t\}\le2\exp\bigl(-\tfrac{t^{2}/2}{\operatorname{Var}(\sum_\nu X_\nu)+At/3}\bigr)$.
Mohri et al. state the one-sided version for the mean, with
$X_\nu\le A$ from above only (Exercise D.4, Eq. D.25, p. 378); with
$t$ equal to $n$ times the deviation of the mean, it is the same
bound. Unlike Hoeffding's, this bound uses the variance.
:::

Apply @eq-fs-bernstein to the centred cell counts. Let $L_0$ be the
$\psi_1$ norm of the centred count of gene $g$ in one bulk cell, and
$L_j$ that of one reference cell of type $j$. The union bound behind
@eq-fs-range-tail then gives (our derivation)

$$
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t\bigr)
\le
2\exp\Bigl[-\gamma\,n_i\min\Bigl(\frac{t^{2}}{4L_0^{2}},\frac{t}{2L_0}\Bigr)\Bigr]
+2\sum_{j=1}^{J}\exp\Bigl[-\gamma\,C_j\min\Bigl(\frac{t^{2}}{4L_j^{2}},\frac{t}{2L_j}\Bigr)\Bigr].
$$ {#eq-fs-range-subexp}

<!-- chk: V20c -->
For $t\le2L$ each term is a Gaussian tail, the shape of
@eq-fs-range-tail with the range $A_g$ replaced by the $\psi_1$ norm
and an unknown constant; for $t\ge2L$ it is an exponential tail, linear
in $t$. Under NB counts the tail of @eq-fs-rnasieve-12 is therefore
sub-exponential in $t$, and the sub-Gaussian decay that RNA-Sieve
states holds only for small $t$ (our remark). A bulk cell is a mixture
of types; its uncentred $\psi_1$ norm is at most the largest norm of
the types, so $L_0$ is finite for NB types whatever the composition
(our remark).

**An explicit bound for NB cells.** The constant $\gamma$ is unknown,
so @eq-fs-range-subexp gives the shape of the tail but no threshold.
For the mean $\bar X$ of $n$ independent NB cells with mean $m$ and
size $\psi$, Markov's inequality applied to $e^{un\bar X}$ and the exact
@eq-fs-nb-mgf give the Cramér–Chernoff bounds (our derivation)

$$
\mathbb{P}(\bar X-m\ge t)\le e^{-nK^{\ast}(m+t)},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(\bar X-m\le-t)\le e^{-nK^{\ast}(m-t)},
\qquad
K^{\ast}(\bar x)=\sup_{u<-\log\pi}\bigl[u\bar x-\log M(u)\bigr],
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-chernoff}

<!-- chk: V20c -->
for $t>0$. The supremum is attained at
$e^{u^{\ast}}=\bar x(m+\psi)/\{m(\bar x+\psi)\}$ and has the closed form
(our derivation)

$$
K^{\ast}(\bar x)=\bar x\log\frac{\bar x(m+\psi)}{m(\bar x+\psi)}+\psi\log\frac{m+\psi}{\bar x+\psi},
\qquad \bar x\ge0,
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-rate}

<!-- chk: V20c -->
with $0\log0=0$ and $K^{\ast}(\bar x)=+\infty$ for $\bar x<0$.
$K^{\ast}$ is convex, with $K^{\ast}(m)=0$ and
$K^{\ast}(0)=\psi\log(1+m/\psi)=-\log\mathbb{P}(X=0)$. As
$\psi\to\infty$, $K^{\ast}(\bar x)\to\bar x\log(\bar x/m)-\bar x+m$, the
Poisson rate. The union bound applied to $\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g$ then
gives, with $K^{\ast}_j$ the rate of type $j$ and $K^{\ast}_0$ that of
a bulk cell,

$$
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t\bigr)
\le
\sum_{\pm}e^{-n_iK^{\ast}_0(\operatorname{E}\tilde y_{g}\pm t/2)}
+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{\pm}e^{-C_jK^{\ast}_j(\tilde\mu_{gj}\pm t/2)}.
$$ {#eq-fs-range-chernoff}

<!-- chk: V20c -->
For the bulk mixture, $K^{\ast}_0$ has no closed form and is a
one-dimensional numerical maximisation. Like the precise tail bounds
RNA-Sieve mentions, @eq-fs-range-chernoff needs the true parameters
(composition, means and sizes).

### Five tail statements for the discrepancy {#sec-fs-five-bounds}

The range distance @eq-fs-rnasieve-12 does not use the composition and
loses power through the union bound. The discrepancy
@eq-fs-discrepancy uses it, and its law has an exact cumulant
generating function under NB counts. The five statements below are
exactly those implemented in `scripts/figures/fig_03_1_tail_bounds.R`;
they are ordered by increasing complexity and labelled T1 to T5 as in
the figures. They hold under four assumptions, for one gene $g$ and one
bulk sample $i$ (index $i$ dropped, $D=D_{gi}$).

- **(A1) Cells.** Counts of different cells are independent. A cell of
  type $j$ has an NB count with mean $\tilde\mu_{gj}$ and size
  $\psi_g$, $\pi_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}/(\tilde\mu_{gj}+\psi_g)$
  (@eq-fs-nb-mgf).
- **(A2) Composition.** The bulk contains exactly $m_{j}=p_jn$ cells of
  type $j$ (fixed integers).
- **(A3) Platforms.** Bulk and reference cells of type $j$ have the same
  law: $a_i=1$, no gene-wise platform ratio, no extra overdispersion.
  Bulk and reference are independent.
- **(A4) Known parameters.** $\boldsymbol p$, $\tilde\mu_{g\cdot}$ and
  $\psi_g$ are known, so $\hat p_j=p_j$ in @eq-fs-discrepancy. No
  statement below accounts for estimated parameters (@sec-fs-plugin).

Under (A1)–(A4), $D=\tilde y_{g}-\sum_jp_j\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}$ is a sum
of $n$ independent bulk terms and $C_j$ independent reference terms per
type, with

$$
\operatorname{E}D=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}D=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{p_j\sigma_{gj}^2}{n}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{p_j^2\sigma_{gj}^2}{C_j},
$$ {#eq-fs-var-d}

<!-- chk: V31a -->
and cumulant generating function

$$
K_D(u)=\log\operatorname{E}e^{uD}
=\sum_{j=1}^{J}m_{j}K_{gj}\Bigl(\frac{u}{n}\Bigr)
+\sum_{j=1}^{J}C_jK_{gj}\Bigl(-\frac{u\,p_j}{C_j}\Bigr),
\qquad
K_{gj}(u)=-\psi_g\log\Bigl(1-\frac{\tilde\mu_{gj}}{\psi_g}\bigl(e^{u}-1\bigr)\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-fs-cgf-d}

<!-- chk: V29a -->
$K_{gj}$ the per-cell cumulant generating function of type $j$
(@eq-fs-nb-mgf), defined for $u_-<u<u_+$ with
$u_+=n\min_j(-\log\pi_{gj})$ and $u_-=\max_jC_j\log\pi_{gj}/p_j<0$.
$K_D$ is convex with $K_D(0)=K_D'(0)=0$. Its Legendre transforms

$$
K_D^{+}(t)=\sup_{0<u<u_+}\bigl[ut-K_D(u)\bigr],
\qquad
K_D^{-}(t)=\sup_{u_-<u<0}\bigl[-ut-K_D(u)\bigr],
\qquad t>0,
$$ {#eq-fs-legendre}

<!-- chk: V29b -->
are computed at the root of $K_D'(u)=\pm t$. The threshold $t_{0.01}$
of a statement is the smallest $t$ at which its tail probability, or
its bound, equals $\alpha/2=0.01$; for a Chernoff bound this means
$K_D^{\pm}(t_{0.01})=\log100$. The reference means are averages over
few cells, so the reference term dominates the third cumulant of $D$
and $D$ is left-skewed in the simulation (skewness $-0.08$ and $-0.06$):
its lower tail is the heavier one.

**Modules.** For a module $M$ of $\lvert M\rvert$ genes, two further
assumptions describe the dependence between genes. Let
$\mathcal{H}=(M,\mathcal{E})$ be a gene graph with maximal degree
$d_{\max}$ and mean degree $\bar d=2\lvert\mathcal{E}\rvert/\lvert M\rvert$.

- **(A5) Within-cell correlation.** In one cell of any type, the counts
  of genes $g$ and $h$ have correlation $\varrho$ when
  $(g,h)\in\mathcal{E}$ and 0 otherwise; different cells are
  independent.
- **(A6) Dependency graph.** Sets of genes with no edge between them
  have independent counts in every cell. Genes of an independent set of
  $\mathcal{H}$ are then mutually independent.

With $c_{ghj}=\varrho\,\sigma_{gj}\sigma_{hj}$ on an edge, and since bulk
and reference are independent,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(D_g,D_h)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{p_j\,c_{ghj}}{n}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{p_j^2\,c_{ghj}}{C_j},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}S_M=\lvert M\rvert+2\sum_{(g,h)\in\mathcal{E}}\operatorname{Corr}(D_g,D_h),
$$ {#eq-fs-module-var}

<!-- chk: V31b -->
with $S_M=\sum_{g\in M}Z_g$, $Z_g=D_g/\operatorname{sd}D_g$ and
$\operatorname{Corr}(D_g,D_h)\le\varrho$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. In the
simulation ($\lvert M\rvert=20$ genes, 30 edges, $d_{\max}=6$,
$\bar d=3$, $\varrho=0.3$), $\operatorname{Var}S_M=37.2$ against 20
for independent genes. The statements below were written for graphs
with $d_{\max}\le10$ and $\bar d\le3$.

::: {#thm-fs-clt}
## T1, Lindeberg–Feller Gaussian approximation

Under (A1)–(A4), $D$ is a sum of independent terms that are identically
distributed within each of $2J$ groups, with finite variances, and a
term of type $j$ carries at most a fraction $1/m_j$ (bulk) or $1/C_j$
(reference) of $\operatorname{Var}D$. As every $m_j$ and every $C_j$
grow with $\boldsymbol p$ fixed, Lindeberg's condition holds and
$D/\operatorname{sd}D$ converges in law to $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. The
approximation used is

$$
\mathbb{P}(D\ge t)\approx1-\Phi\Bigl(\frac{t}{\operatorname{sd}D}\Bigr),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(D\le-t)\approx\Phi\Bigl(-\frac{t}{\operatorname{sd}D}\Bigr),
\qquad
t_{0.01}=z_{0.99}\operatorname{sd}D,
$$ {#eq-fs-clt}

with $z_{0.99}=2.326$ and $\operatorname{sd}D$ from @eq-fs-var-d. It is
an approximation, not a bound: no error term is evaluated, and it is
symmetric in the two tails.
:::

RNA-Sieve's likelihood rests on this Gaussian approximation
[@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021, Eqs 5, 7, 9]. The
Lindeberg argument above is ours and is not machine-checked.

::: {#cor-fs-clt-log}
## T1-log, log-normal approximation of the ratio

Let $R=\tilde y_{g}\big/\sum_jp_j\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}$ and
$\bar\mu_g=\sum_jp_j\tilde\mu_{gj}$, with $\tilde y_g>0$. To first
order (delta method), $\log R\approx D/\bar\mu_g$ and
$\operatorname{Var}\log R\approx\operatorname{Var}D/\bar\mu_g^{2}$.
Taking $\log R$ Gaussian and centred at 0, and replacing the random
denominator by $\bar\mu_g$, gives the thresholds

$$
t_{0.01}^{+}=\bar\mu_g\bigl(e^{z_{0.99}\operatorname{sd}D/\bar\mu_g}-1\bigr),
\qquad
t_{0.01}^{-}=\bar\mu_g\bigl(1-e^{-z_{0.99}\operatorname{sd}D/\bar\mu_g}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-fs-clt-log}

It is an approximation in three steps (delta method, normality of
$\log R$ without the $-\operatorname{Var}\log R/2$ shift, fixed
denominator), not a bound.
:::

The log-ratio form matches RNA-Sieve's bulk-to-reference ratio, one of
its four MAD statistics; RNA-Sieve itself prints no log-scale central
limit theorem. Gibrat's law does not apply: it gives a log-normal limit
for a *product* of many independent factors, and a bulk is a *sum* of
cells. The log-normal shape here comes only from the delta method. In
the simulation the variance step is accurate (Monte Carlo
$\operatorname{sd}\log R=0.0601$ against $0.0600$ from the formula for
the low-expression gene), but the shape is not: the approximation
implies a right-skewed ratio, whereas $D$ is left-skewed, so T1-log
errs on the anti-conservative side in the lower tail.

::: {#thm-fs-dep-clt}
## T2, Gaussian approximation on a dependency graph

Under (A1)–(A6), $\mathcal{H}$ is a dependency graph for
$(Z_g)_{g\in M}$, and the approximation used is

$$
\mathbb{P}(S_M\ge t)\approx1-\Phi\Bigl(\frac{t}{\sigma_S}\Bigr),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(S_M\le-t)\approx\Phi\Bigl(-\frac{t}{\sigma_S}\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-fs-dep-clt}

with $\sigma_S^2=\operatorname{Var}S_M$ of @eq-fs-module-var.

Baldi & Rinott (1989) and Chen & Shao (2004, Theorem 2.7) bound the
error of this normal approximation in terms of the maximal degree and
of moments above the second. That error bound is not evaluated here.
:::

[TODO-cite: Baldi & Rinott 1989, On normal approximations of distributions in terms of dependency graphs, Ann. Probab. 17(4)]{.highlight}
[TODO-cite: Chen & Shao 2004, Normal approximation under local dependence, Ann. Probab. 32(3A):1985-2028, doi:10.1214/009117904000000450]{.highlight}
The Gaussian approximation with $\operatorname{Var}S_M=\lvert M\rvert$,
which ignores the edges, is T1 for the module. The bound of Chen & Shao
is the result that MEAD uses for its central limit theorem across genes
(@sec-fs-appendix).

::: {#thm-fs-poisson}
## T3, Chernoff bound with Poisson cumulant generating functions

Replace each $K_{gj}$ in @eq-fs-cgf-d by the Poisson cumulant
generating function $\tilde\mu_{gj}(e^{u}-1)$:

$$
K^{\mathrm{Pois}}_D(u)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}m_{j}\tilde\mu_{gj}\bigl(e^{u/n}-1\bigr)
+\sum_{j=1}^{J}C_j\tilde\mu_{gj}\bigl(e^{-up_j/C_j}-1\bigr),
\qquad u\in\mathbb{R}.
$$ {#eq-fs-cgf-pois}

<!-- chk: V29c -->
If the counts are Poisson ($\psi_g=\infty$) and (A1)–(A4) hold, then
for $t>0$, with the transforms @eq-fs-legendre of $K^{\mathrm{Pois}}_D$,
$\mathbb{P}(D\ge t)\le\exp\{-K^{\mathrm{Pois},+}_D(t)\}$ and
$\mathbb{P}(D\le-t)\le\exp\{-K^{\mathrm{Pois},-}_D(t)\}$. For a single
sum of $n$ cells with mean $m$ (no reference term), the rate has the
closed form $n\{\bar x\log(\bar x/m)-\bar x+m\}$ at $\bar x=m\pm t$.
Under NB counts the statement is not a bound: the Poisson model
understates the per-cell variance by the factor
$1+\tilde\mu_{gj}/\psi_g$.
:::

<!-- chk: V29d -->
For the module, T3 adds the transforms over genes as if they were
independent, with the NB standard deviations in $Z_g$; it is then
misspecified twice (Poisson margins, independence).

::: {#thm-fs-nb}
## T4, Chernoff bound with the exact NB cumulant generating function

Under (A1)–(A4), for every $t>0$ and every $n$, $C_j$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(D\ge t)\le\exp\bigl\{-K_D^{+}(t)\bigr\},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(D\le-t)\le\exp\bigl\{-K_D^{-}(t)\bigr\},
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-bound}

with $K_D^{\pm}$ the transforms @eq-fs-legendre of the exact
@eq-fs-cgf-d. The bound follows from Markov's inequality applied to
$e^{uD}$; its prefactor is 1 and it has no unknown constant, unlike
@eq-fs-bernstein and @eq-fs-range-subexp.
:::

With $J=1$ and no reference noise ($C_1=\infty$), T4 reduces to
@eq-fs-nb-chernoff with $n$ bulk cells. For the module, T4 sums the
cumulant generating functions $K_{D_g}(u/\operatorname{sd}D_g)$ over
genes: it is a finite-sample bound if the genes are independent, and it
is not under (A5) with $\varrho>0$.

::: {#thm-fs-nb-dep}
## T5, NB Chernoff bound after a proper colouring, after Janson

Under (A1)–(A4) for every gene and (A6), let
$\mathcal{M}_1,\dots,\mathcal{M}_{\chi_G}$ be a proper colouring of
$\mathcal{H}$, that is a partition of $M$ into $\chi_G$ classes with no
edge inside a class. One exists with

$$
\chi_G\le\bar\chi_G=\min\Bigl(d_{\max}+1,\ \frac{1+\sqrt{8\lvert\mathcal{E}\rvert+1}}{2}\Bigr).
$$ {#eq-fs-colouring}

<!-- chk: V30b -->
By convexity of the exponential and independence within each class,
for every $u$ in the domain,

$$
\operatorname{E}e^{uS_M}
\le\frac{1}{\chi_G}\sum_{c=1}^{\chi_G}\prod_{g\in\mathcal{M}_c}\operatorname{E}e^{\chi_GuZ_g}
=\exp\bar K_S(u),
\qquad
\bar K_S(u)=\log\Bigl(\frac{1}{\chi_G}\sum_{c=1}^{\chi_G}\exp\sum_{g\in\mathcal{M}_c}K_{D_g}\Bigl(\frac{\chi_Gu}{\operatorname{sd}D_g}\Bigr)\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-fs-janson}

<!-- chk: V30a -->
and therefore, for $t>0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(S_M\ge t)\le\inf_{u>0}\exp\{-ut+\bar K_S(u)\},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(S_M\le-t)\le\inf_{u<0}\exp\{ut+\bar K_S(u)\},
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-dep}

with $\chi_Gu/\operatorname{sd}D_g$ inside the domain of every
$K_{D_g}$. The bound holds for any dependence between colour classes,
does not use $\varrho$, and has no unknown constant.
:::

[TODO-cite: Janson 2004, Large deviations for sums of partly dependent random variables, Random Struct. Algorithms 24(3), doi:10.1002/rsa.20008]{.highlight}
Both degree conditions enter through $\chi_G$: the maximal degree through
$d_{\max}+1$, the number of edges, hence the mean degree, through the
second term of @eq-fs-colouring. The greedy colouring with vertices in
decreasing degree order (Welsh & Powell 1967)
[TODO-cite: Welsh & Powell 1967, An upper bound for the chromatic number of a graph, Comput. J. 10(1)]{.highlight}
attains both bounds (our remark); in the simulation it uses
$\chi_G=3$ classes of 8, 7 and 5 genes, against $\bar\chi_G=7$. The price of
the colouring is the factor $\chi_G$ inside the argument: near $u=0$,
$\bar K_S(u)\approx \chi_G\lvert M\rvert u^{2}/2$, an effective variance
of 60 against $\operatorname{Var}S_M=37.2$. Janson (2004) states the
bound for fractional covers by independent sets with weights; the
equal-weight proper colouring is the special case used here (this
remark is not checked against the paper). The dependent Bernstein
inequality of Zhang & Li, used by DECALS, has a constant equal to
$\bar\chi_G$ and an unknown absolute constant in the exponent
(@eq-fs-bernstein-dep, @sec-fs-appendix).
