The Monte Carlo interval is the 95 % order-statistic interval of the empirical quantile. A dash means that the statement does not apply to that unit. Seed 20261101. {#tbl-fs-thresholds}

Read from @tbl-fs-thresholds:

- **Most conservative.** Per gene, T4 has the largest threshold in all
  four panels, 1.29 to 1.33 times the Monte Carlo one. Per module, T5
  has the largest, 1.70 to 1.72 times.
- **Least conservative.** T3 has the smallest threshold for the
  high-expression gene (a quarter of the Monte Carlo one) and for the
  module. For the low-expression gene, whose variance factor
  $1+\tilde\mu_{gj}/\psi_g$ is at most 1.3, T3 is the second most
  conservative statement.
- **Under-coverage.** A threshold below the Monte Carlo interval
  rejects more than 1 % of consistent genes in that tail. This happens
  for T1 and T1-log in the lower tail of both genes, for T3 in both
  tails of the high-expression gene, for T1, T3 and T4 in both tails of
  the module, and for T2 in the lower tail of the module (0.8 % below
  Monte Carlo). Only the two finite-sample bounds whose assumptions hold,
  T4 for one gene and T5 for a module, never under-cover.
- **Far tail.** In a separate run with the same seed, the T4 to Monte
  Carlo ratio falls from 1.29–1.33 at $0.01$ to 1.11–1.14 at $10^{-5}$,
  and the lower-tail T1 ratio from 0.98 to 0.94–0.95: the Gaussian
  under-coverage grows further out.

**Multiplicity.** The level $\alpha/2=0.01$ per side is per gene. Over
about 3,000 genes a correctly calibrated filter flags about 60
consistent genes at this level. A Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg
correction moves the threshold into the far tail, where the Gaussian
statements under-cover more and the Chernoff bounds come closer to the
truth.

::: {#nte-fs-quantile-regression .callout-note}
## Link with non-parametric quantile regression

Each statement bounds or approximates the $(1-\alpha/2)$ quantile of
$\lvert D_g\rvert$ under a count model, gene by gene. Quantile
regression (Koenker & Bassett 1978)
[TODO-cite: Koenker & Bassett 1978, Regression quantiles, Econometrica 46(1):33-50, doi:10.2307/1913643]{.highlight}
estimates the conditional quantile $Q_{1-\alpha/2}(\tilde y_{gi}\mid\hat y_{gi})$
of the bulk given the fitted bulk
$\hat y_{gi}=\sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}$, pooled across genes
and without a count model. Conformalised quantile regression (Romano,
Patterson & Candès 2019)
[TODO-cite: Romano, Patterson & Candès 2019, Conformalized quantile regression, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32, arXiv:1905.03222]{.highlight}
adds a finite-sample coverage guarantee under exchangeability of the
genes. Genes differ in mean and are correlated, so that guarantee is
marginal over genes, not per gene. The two approaches answer the same
question with different assumptions: the bounds need a correct model
and known parameters, the band needs exchangeable genes. The
reproducibility book compares the flags of all five statements with
such a band on the Suppinger data.
:::

### Plug-in parameters {#sec-fs-plugin}

Assumption (A4) never holds in practice. The application plugs in the
following estimates.

- **Composition.** $\hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i}$ comes from
  deMixSC-style iterated weighted NNLS of $\tilde y_{gi}$ on the
  reference means, with weights
  $w_{gi}^{-1}=\hat y_{gi}^{2}+(\tilde y_{gi}-\hat y_{gi})^{2}+c_w$,
  $c_w=2$ [@guoDeMixSCDeconvolutionFramework2023, Eq. 4, PDF p. 12].
  deMixSC also splits the genes into a low-discrepancy set and a
  high-discrepancy set $\mathcal{G}_2$ whose residuals are
  down-weighted. $\mathcal{G}_2$ is empty here: deMixSC builds it from a
  benchmark of bulk and single-nucleus data from the same aliquots (PDF
  p. 11), which a one-specimen reference lacks.
- **Scale.** $a_i$ is the sum of the NNLS coefficients, which estimate
  $a_ip_{ji}$; $\hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i}$ is the normalised
  coefficient vector.
- **Dispersion.** $\psi_g$ comes from the reference fit of tier (ii),
  and the extra overdispersion between platforms is fixed at 1 (none).
- **Platform ratio.** $\tilde b_g=1$ for every gene (assumption A3).
  @sec-fs-platform-ratio replaces it by a plug-in estimate.

With these plug-ins every statement is approximate, including T4 and
T5: they are exact only at the true parameters. Because
$\hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i}$ is fitted to the same bulk, the fitted
discrepancies are expected to be smaller than under the true
composition, so the plug-in thresholds should err on the conservative
side for genes that do not drive the fit (our remark, not checked by
simulation).

### Plug-in gene-wise platform ratio {#sec-fs-platform-ratio}

Every statement above tests $D_{gi}$ against the spread allowed by A3:
the same per-cell mean on both platforms. A full-length bulk library
yields reads in proportion to the number of molecules times the
transcript length, whereas a 3′ UMI library counts molecules
[TODO-cite: Oshlack & Wakefield 2009, Transcript length bias in RNA-seq data confounds systems biology, Biology Direct 4:14, doi:10.1186/1745-6150-4-14]{.highlight}.
Full-length single-cell protocols show the same length bias as bulk
RNA-seq, and UMI protocols do not
[TODO-cite: Phipson, Zappia & Oshlack 2017, Gene length and detection bias in single cell RNA sequencing protocols, F1000Research 6:595, doi:10.12688/f1000research.11290.1]{.highlight}.
Between such a bulk and a 3′ reference, A3 therefore fails gene by
gene, and so do the tail statements. The relaxed mean is

$$
\operatorname{E}\Bigl(\frac{\tilde y_{gi}}{a_i}\Bigr)
=\tilde b_g\sum_{j=1}^{J}p_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj},
$$ {#eq-fs-platform-mean}

with one ratio $\tilde b_g$ per gene (notation of
[2.1, alignment](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-alignment)).
Length predicts $\log_2\tilde b_g=\log_2L_g+\text{const}$, with $L_g$
the mean transcript length: a slope of 1. With a plug-in $\hat b_g$
the discrepancy and the range statistic become

$$
D^{b}_{gi}=\frac{\tilde y_{gi}}{a_i\hat b_g}-\sum_{j=1}^{J}\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj},
\qquad
\delta^{\mathrm{R},b}_g
=\inf\Bigl\{\bigl\lvert\tilde y_{gi}/\hat b_g-a\bigr\rvert:\ \min_{j}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\le a\le\max_{j}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\Bigr\},
$$ {#eq-fs-discrepancy-b}

and $(a_i,\hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i})$ are fitted on
$\tilde y_{gi}/\hat b_g$.

<!-- chk: V36a -->
**Ratio known.** If $\hat b_g=\tilde b_g$, then
$\tilde y_{gi}/\tilde b_g$ is a sum of $a_i$ cells of the reference
law, so $D^{b}_{gi}$ has the cumulant generating function
@eq-fs-cgf-d with $n=a_i$. The thresholds of T1 to T5 are unchanged.

<!-- chk: V36b -->
**Ratio estimated.** Write $\hat b_g=\tilde b_ge^{\varepsilon_g}$ with
$\operatorname{E}\varepsilon_g=0$ and
$\operatorname{Var}\varepsilon_g=v_g$, and let $\varepsilon_g$ be
independent of the bulk sample under test. Then, to first order in
$v_g$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}D^{b}_{gi}
\approx\operatorname{Var}D_{gi}
+\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{J}p_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}\Bigr)^{2}v_g .
$$ {#eq-fs-var-b}

The expansion also has a term $2v_g\operatorname{Var}D_{gi}$, small
relative to $\operatorname{Var}D_{gi}$ when $v_g$ is small, and a bias
$v_g\sum_jp_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}/2$. Both are dropped. The extra term of
@eq-fs-var-b enters the standardised discrepancy and the Gaussian
statement T1. The Chernoff statements T3 to T5 are then conditional on
$\hat b_g$: they treat it as known.

<!-- chk: V36c -->
**Identifiability.** The plug-in is defined only under four
conditions.

- **Diagonal.** One scale per gene, $\tilde{\mathbf B}=\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol b})$:
  length and capture act on each gene separately. The competition
  between genes for reads within a library is a common factor, which
  $a_i$ absorbs.
- **Up to a common factor.** Multiplying every $\tilde b_g$ by $c$ and
  $a_i$ by $1/c$ leaves @eq-fs-platform-mean unchanged, so a
  normalisation is needed, for example
  $\operatorname{median}_g\log\hat b_g=0$.
- **Not from the sample under test.** With one sample and free
  $\tilde{\boldsymbol b}$, any composition $\boldsymbol p'$ fits every
  mean with
  $\tilde b'_g=\tilde b_g\sum_jp_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}/\sum_jp'_j\tilde\mu_{gj}$:
  the ratio absorbs the residual
  ([2.1, identifiability](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-plugin-identifiability);
  MEAD, Theorem 1).
- **From samples whose compositions differ.** $\tilde b_g$ cancels from
  the ratio of the means of one gene in two samples, so a pool of bulk
  samples of different compositions carries the information on
  $\boldsymbol p$. Cross-fitting uses this: the ratio applied to one
  sample is estimated on the other samples only. This also makes
  $\varepsilon_g$ independent of that sample, as @eq-fs-var-b requires.

A ratio that depends on both the gene and the type, $\tilde b_{gj}$, is
confounded with $\tilde\mu_{gj}$ and is not identified without paired
measurements of each type on both platforms.

**Estimators.** Three routes give $\hat b_g$ under these conditions.

- **Moment ratio on a pool.** Alternate the deMixSC plug-in on
  $\tilde y_{gi}/\hat b_g$ with
  $\log\hat b_g=\operatorname{median}_i\log\{(\tilde y_{gi}/a_i)/\sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\}$
  over the pooled samples. This is the
  first stage of `RCTD`, which fits a gene-wise platform effect on a
  pseudo-bulk of all spots and then holds it fixed
  [@cableRobustDecompositionCell2022a, pp. 3, 6–7]. $v_g$ is the
  variance of the log ratios over the pooled samples, divided by their
  number.
- **Length model.** $\log\hat b_g=f(\log_2L_g)$, with $f$ a smooth
  function fitted on the pool. It has few parameters, so it is
  identified from fewer samples, but it leaves every effect other than
  length in the residual.
- **Transport between pseudo-bulk and bulk.** With paired pseudo-bulk
  and bulk samples, a gene-wise affine map is the `Bisque` estimator
  [@jewAccurateEstimationCell2020]. Its multivariate version is a
  Gaussian transport map
  ([2.1, pairing route](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-av-linear);
  [5.1, two-scale transport](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-bisque-ot)).
  Restricted to a diagonal, the map reduces to one scale per gene, the
  moment ratio above. It needs several pairs per gene.

The filter applies only if the residual discrepancy remains after
dividing by a cross-fitted $\hat b_g$: a gene whose ratio is stable
across samples is a platform effect to model, not a defect. The
reproducibility book compares, on the Suppinger data, no ratio, a length
model and a gene-wise ratio, all cross-fitted over three matched times.


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Tier (iv): down-weighting by the model {#sec-fs-weighting}

Filters remove genes; a weighted likelihood keeps them and lets their
variance decide their influence. The reviewed methods sit on a ladder of
noise models (@tbl-fs-ladder; full ladder in
[5.1](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html)).

| Rung | Variance of the bulk residual | Methods (anchors) |
|---|---|---|
| Weighted least squares | diagonal, gene-wise weights | MuSiC: bulk noise plus cross-subject variance, Eq. 10, p. 7; DWLS: fitted values, capped by a dampening constant, pp. 2, 7; SCDC: maximal-variance weights, clipped, pp. 5, 10; deMixSC: $\hat y^2$ plus squared residual plus a constant, p. 12; MEAD: reference variance with empirical-Bayes shrinkage, pp. 17–18 |
| Generalised least squares | full gene–gene covariance, depends on $\boldsymbol{p}$ | DeCovarT: $\sum_jp_j^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ (population) or $\sum_jp_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ (single cell); DECALS: $\sum_jp_{ji}^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ for inference, pp. 7, 9 |
| Feasible GLS | covariance estimated, then iterated with $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ | DECALS Algorithm 1, p. 9; DeCovarT plug-in $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$ |
| Sandwich / GEE | working covariance, robust variance | MEAD: sandwich over a dependence set, pp. 13, 18 |

: Down-weighting classes in the reviewed methods. Page anchors refer to the PDFs extracted for this review. {#tbl-fs-ladder}

Two observations follow.

- DECALS computes its point estimate by constrained *ordinary* least
  squares and uses the covariance only for inference, because a GLS fit
  with an estimated covariance per sample was biased in their
  experiments [@caiStatisticalInferenceCelltype2024, p. 6]. The same risk
  applies to any feasible GLS whose covariance is estimated on few cells;
  shrinkage of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$ addresses it
  ([3.2](03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html)).
- MEAD notes that removing genes brings no efficiency gain unless their
  noise levels differ [@xieStatisticalInferenceCell2026, p. 17]. Once the
  covariance is in the model, hard filtering is needed only for genes
  outside the model's support: the presence gate (@sec-fs-presence)
  and, when a matched bulk exists, the cross-platform outliers of tier
  (iii) (@sec-fs-cross-platform).


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Selection effect on the covariance {#sec-fs-selection-effect}

Selecting genes changes the covariance that is then estimated on them.

- **Small within-type variance by construction.** A ratio such as
  $\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{B},g}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{W},g}$ of @eq-fs-ss
  rewards a small within-type part. ReDeconv goes further and keeps the
  genes with the smallest coefficient of variation
  [@luTranscriptomeSizeMatters2025, p. 14]; MuSiC's tree-guided stage
  keeps genes with small intra-cluster variance
  [@wangBulkTissueCell2019, p. 8]. A panel chosen this way removes much
  of the within-type covariance that DeCovarT models, and the estimated
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ on that panel is close to diagonal for that
  reason, not because genes are conditionally independent
  ([3.2](03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html)).
- **Weak marginal effects hide interactions.** Genes with weak marginal
  effects are dropped by every univariate screen, and gene pairs whose
  signal lies in their covariance, not in their means, are then never
  examined. Covariance-aware criteria (@sec-optimal-design,
  @sec-pareto-panel) can recover them only from a shortlist that still
  contains them.

Screening on marginal effects first is the practice that the design of
experiments justifies with three principles (Wu & Hamada 2021, §4.6)
[TODO-cite: Wu & Hamada 2021, Experiments: Planning, Analysis, and Optimization, 3rd ed., Wiley, Section 4.6 (no DOI)]{.highlight}.
Effect sparsity says that few effects are active (Box & Meyer 1986)
[TODO-cite: Box & Meyer 1986, An analysis for unreplicated fractional factorials, Technometrics 28(1), doi:10.1080/00401706.1986.10488093]{.highlight}.
Effect hierarchy says that main effects are more likely to be active
than two-factor interactions, and these more than higher-order ones.
Effect heredity says that an interaction is active only if one (weak
heredity) or both (strong heredity) of its parent main effects are
active; it guides the analysis of designs with complex aliasing
(Hamada & Wu 1992) and the priors of Bayesian variable selection with
related predictors (Chipman 1996)
[TODO-cite: Hamada & Wu 1992, Analysis of designed experiments with complex aliasing, J. Qual. Technol. 24(3), doi:10.1080/00224065.1992.11979383]{.highlight}
[TODO-cite: Chipman 1996, Bayesian variable selection with related predictors, Can. J. Stat. 24(1), doi:10.2307/3315687]{.highlight}.
The marginality principle of linear models, that a model with an
interaction should contain the main effects it involves, is the
model-building counterpart (Nelder 1977)
[TODO-cite: Nelder 1977, A reformulation of linear models, J. R. Stat. Soc. A 140(1), doi:10.2307/2344517]{.highlight}.

- **Empirical support.** The principles were checked on published
  experiments: a meta-analysis of 113 factorial data sets (Li,
  Sudarsanam & Frey 2006) and a meta-analysis of response-surface
  experiments (Ockuly et al. 2017)
  [TODO-cite: Li, Sudarsanam & Frey 2006, Regularities in data from factorial experiments, Complexity 11(5), doi:10.1002/cplx.20123]{.highlight}
  [TODO-cite: Ockuly et al. 2017, Response surface experiments: a meta-analysis, Chemometr. Intell. Lab. Syst. 164, doi:10.1016/j.chemolab.2017.03.009]{.highlight}.
  Their estimated frequencies are not quoted here; they are to be read
  from the papers.
- **Methods built on heredity.** The lasso for hierarchical
  interactions enforces heredity as a constraint (Bien, Taylor &
  Tibshirani 2013), and interaction screening for ultrahigh-dimensional
  data searches interactions among the variables kept by a marginal
  screen (Hao & Zhang 2014)
  [TODO-cite: Bien, Taylor & Tibshirani 2013, A lasso for hierarchical interactions, Ann. Stat. 41(3), doi:10.1214/13-AOS1096]{.highlight}
  [TODO-cite: Hao & Zhang 2014, Interaction screening for ultrahigh-dimensional data, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 109, doi:10.1080/01621459.2014.881741]{.highlight}.
- **Counter-examples.** Sure independence screening misses variables
  that are marginally uncorrelated with the response but jointly
  important, which motivated its iterated version (Fan & Lv 2008).
  Genetic models can show epistasis with no main effect at all
  (Culverhouse et al. 2002). Differential networking describes genes
  whose connections change between conditions while their expression
  level does not (de la Fuente 2010)
  [TODO-cite: Fan & Lv 2008, Sure independence screening for ultrahigh dimensional feature space, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 70(5), doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00674.x]{.highlight}
  [TODO-cite: Culverhouse, Suarez, Lin & Reich 2002, A perspective on epistasis: limits of models displaying no main effect, Am. J. Hum. Genet. 70(2), doi:10.1086/338759]{.highlight}
  [TODO-cite: de la Fuente 2010, From 'differential expression' to 'differential networking', Trends Genet. 26(7), doi:10.1016/j.tig.2010.05.001]{.highlight}.

[Heredity is an empirical regularity, a default assumption rather than
a theorem, and it fails precisely for covariance-only
signal.]{.mark} A gene pair whose types differ only in their
correlation has no parent main effect, so a marginal screen followed by
a heredity-constrained search cannot find it.

A practical check is to compare the distribution of $v_{gj}$, and of the
off-diagonal entries of $\boldsymbol{V}_j$, between the selected panel
and the genes that pass the presence gate.


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Perspectives {#sec-perspectives}

## Cross-sample consistency {#sec-fs-cross-sample}

Cross-sample consistency compares a gene across specimens, the subjects
or donors of the reference. It needs at least two specimens, so a
one-specimen reference cannot assess it.

- **Cross-subject variance (MuSiC).** MuSiC's cross-subject consistency
  guards against the choice of subjects [@wangBulkTissueCell2019, p. 2].
  Its weights down-weight genes with a large cross-subject variance
  (Eq. 10, p. 7), and an optional gene- and subject-specific intercept
  absorbs subject effects (p. 7). With $R\ge2$ donors this variance is
  the between-donor covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}$ of
  [2.1](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-one-replicate).
- **Pseudo-bulk differential expression.** `DESeq2`, `edgeR` or
  `limma`–voom on donor-level pseudo-bulks test a population contrast
  with donors as replicates [@loveModeratedEstimationFold2014a;
  @crowellMuscatDetectsSubpopulationspecific2020]. Appendix S6 uses them
  only for multi-donor references
  ([S6](S6-feature-screening-scenario.html#sec-four-scores)).

Two cell lines profiled in one experiment are the closest available
analogue of two specimens; the reproducibility book has a sensitivity
analysis on the two cell lines at 48 h.

## Cross-technology references {#sec-fs-cross-technology}

Two single-cell references of the same tissue from different
technologies (droplet against plate-based, single-cell against
single-nucleus) measure the same types with different gene-wise capture
efficiencies $b_g$. Their comparison needs no composition: the type
means can be compared type by type, so the range and discrepancy
statistics of @sec-fs-range-tail reduce to differences
$\hat{\tilde\mu}^{(1)}_{gj}-\hat{\tilde\mu}^{(2)}_{gj}$, with both
sides estimated from cells. Genes whose ratio
$\hat{\tilde\mu}^{(1)}_{gj}/\hat{\tilde\mu}^{(2)}_{gj}$ varies across
types are inconsistent between technologies whatever the scale; a ratio
constant across types is a gene-wise capture ratio, which MEAD's model
absorbs. This needs a common annotation of the types in both references.

## Dependent cells in a tissue {#sec-fs-dependent-cells}

Assumption (A1) treats the cells of one bulk as independent. In a
tissue, neighbouring cells share a microenvironment, so the counts of a
gene in two neighbouring cells can be correlated. A neighbourhood graph
on the cells of a bulk, gene by gene, would then play the role of the
gene graph $\mathcal{H}$ of @sec-fs-five-bounds. The colouring argument
of @thm-fs-nb-dep applies unchanged to the sum over cells: with the
cells coloured into $\chi_G$ classes of mutually independent cells, the
moment generating function of the bulk total is bounded by the average
over classes of products of per-cell terms evaluated at $\chi_Gu$. The
dependency-graph central limit theorem of @thm-fs-dep-clt applies in
the same way. Spatial transcriptomics would supply the graph; its
maximal degree sets $\chi_G$.

## Covariance-driven (post hoc) feature selection {#sec-fs-multivariate}

The gate of tier (ii) runs before any covariance is estimated, gene by
gene, and uses no per-type characteristic beyond the labels. The
criteria below treat the panel $\mathcal{G}$ as a subset-selection
problem on the full $J$-column signature and use the within-type
covariance or precision matrices, so they can run only after
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$ (or $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j$)
has been estimated on a shortlist
([3.2](03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html),
[3.3](03-3-precision-networks.html)). The likelihood of DeCovarT
depends on $\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}$ and on the covariance
mixture, so this is the geometry of the model; it is also why the stage
is post hoc.

::: {#wrn-fs-circularity .callout-warning}
## Circularity

[A panel optimised for DeCovarT's own information makes DeCovarT's later
performance on that panel uninterpretable: a gain can come from the
panel or from the model.]{.mark} A comparison with other methods must
use a panel chosen without the model, such as the tier (ii) gate, or
report both panels, and every covariance-driven step must be repeated
inside the training folds
([S6](S6-feature-screening-scenario.html#sec-cv-selection)).
:::

### The ANOVA ratio is a screen, not the objective {#sec-fs-screen-objective}

Take $J=2$, one gene, the population model of DeCovarT
([1.2](01-2-population-inference.html#sec-fisher-p)) and equal
within-type variances $\sigma_g^2$. Then
$y_g\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(p\mu_{g1}+(1-p)\mu_{g2},\,\sigma_g^2 s(p)\bigr)$
with $s(p)=p^2+(1-p)^2$, and the Fisher information for $p$ is

$$
I_g(p)
=
\frac{\Delta_g^{2}}{s(p)}
+
\frac12\Bigl(\frac{s'(p)}{s(p)}\Bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\Delta_g=\frac{\mu_{g1}-\mu_{g2}}{\sigma_g}.
$$ {#eq-fs-j2-fisher}

<!-- chk: V4b, V4e, V4f -->
The second term is the same for every gene, so $I_g(p)$ is affine in
$\Delta_g^2$ with a positive slope. Computed on the scale of the model,
the one-way ANOVA ratio
$F_g=\{\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{B},g}/(J-1)\}/\{\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{W},g}/(C-J)\}$
estimates $\Delta_g^2$: $F_g$ is non-central $F_{1,C-2}$ with
non-centrality $\tilde C\Delta_g^{2}$, $\tilde C=C_1C_2/C$, so
$\operatorname{E}F_g\approx1+\tilde C\Delta_g^2$ (exactly, a factor
$\nu/(\nu-2)$ with $\nu=C-2$ multiplies this). Ranking genes by $F_g$
therefore ranks them by $I_g(p)$ at every $p$, and with independent
genes, whose informations add, the top-ranked genes by $F_g$ maximise
the total information $\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}I_g(p)$. [The univariate
ratio is a screen; the objective for a panel is the Fisher information
for $\boldsymbol{p}$ of the whole panel.]{.mark} The ratio ignores:

- **redundancy and collinearity.** Two genes that separate the same pair
  of types add little information together, and concatenated
  one-versus-rest lists inflate the condition number of
  $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}$ (@sec-kappa-limits);
- **the covariance DeCovarT models.** With
  $\sigma_{g1}\ne\sigma_{g2}$ the information depends on $p$ through
  $p^2\sigma_{g1}^2+(1-p)^2\sigma_{g2}^2$, and with correlated genes the
  informations add only at isolated values of the correlation;
- **the count mean–variance relation**, unless the ratio is computed on
  residuals of a model with the right variance function
  (@sec-fs-omnibus).

### Multivariate tests {#sec-fs-multivariate-tests}

A multivariate test would replace the $G$ gene-wise nulls by one null on
the vector $\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}$. Two routes are often confused.

- **Gene-wise GEE is still gene-wise.** GEE extends the quasi-score to a
  vector of correlated observations, with a working covariance
  (Liang & Zeger 1986)
  [TODO-cite: Liang & Zeger 1986, Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models, Biometrika 73:13-22, doi:10.1093/biomet/73.1.13]{.highlight}.
  Fitted once per gene, it still returns $G$ $p$-values and still needs
  FDR control: correlation-aware inference does not remove
  multiplicity.
- **A joint test needs $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$.** A Hotelling or MANOVA
  test of equal type means on the panel uses the within-type covariance,
  which is high-dimensional when $C_j$ is not much larger than
  $|\mathcal{G}|$, as for rare types
  ([3.2](03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html)). With a regularised
  $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$ such a test is possible on a
  shortlist, but its calibration is open. PERMANOVA (@sec-fs-calibration)
  avoids the inverse covariance by permuting a sum of squared distances,
  and a module-level version of the label permutation is a candidate.

#### Variance-weighted condition number {#sec-weighted-kappa}

With gene-wise uncertainties $\tau_g^2$ (biological, sampling and
optional reference-to-bulk discrepancy), standardise the rows and
evaluate the conditioning in the $(J-1)$-dimensional contrast space
induced by $\sum_jp_j=1$:

$$
\kappa_2\bigl(\boldsymbol{T}_{\mathcal{G}}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}\boldsymbol{K}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{T}_{\mathcal{G}}=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_g^2)_{g\in\mathcal{G}},
$$ {#eq-weighted-kappa}

where the $J\times(J-1)$ matrix $\boldsymbol{K}$ has orthonormal columns
orthogonal to $\mathbf{1}$. Unweighted $\kappa_2$ can favour quiet but
biased genes. @eq-weighted-kappa is the square root of the condition
number of the information of @sec-optimal-design with a diagonal
covariance, so it still misses the covariance-only regime in which
DeCovarT identifies types whose means agree
([1.2](01-2-population-inference.html#sec-identifiability)).

### Spectral entropy of a covariance (Unico) {#sec-fs-vn-entropy}

Unico quantifies "the amount of signal coming from the covariance
structure of a given gene" by the von Neumann entropy of the normalised
$J\times J$ matrix of correlations between cell types of that gene
[@chenUnicoUnifiedModelCell2025, pp. 19–20; review in
[5.1](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-unico)]. The covariance
is taken across samples of the cell-type-specific levels of the gene.
The paper prints no formula. Let $\boldsymbol{R}_g$ be that correlation
matrix, with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_J$. A von Neumann
entropy needs a matrix of unit trace, and
$\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R}_g=J$, so we read the definition as
(our reading)

$$
H^{\mathrm{vN}}_g
=-\sum_{h=1}^{J}\tilde\lambda_h\log\tilde\lambda_h
=\log J-\frac1J\sum_{h=1}^{J}\lambda_h\log\lambda_h,
\qquad
\tilde\lambda_h=\frac{\lambda_h}{\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R}_g}=\frac{\lambda_h}{J},
$$ {#eq-fs-vn-entropy}

<!-- chk: V21b -->
with $0\log0=0$. The superscript separates it from the specificity
entropy $H_g$ of @eq-gini. The $\tilde\lambda_h$ form a probability
vector, so $0\le H^{\mathrm{vN}}_g\le\log J$. The maximum $\log J$ is
reached if and only if every $\lambda_h=1$, that is
$\boldsymbol{R}_g=\boldsymbol{I}$. The minimum 0 is reached if and only
if $\boldsymbol{R}_g$ has rank one, that is all cross-type correlations
equal $\pm1$. The paper scales the values "to the range [0,1]" because
the entropy is bounded by a number that depends on the number of cell
types (p. 20); dividing by $\log J$ does this.

Unico states that "High entropy corresponds to cases where no
substantial cell-type covariance structure exists, and low entropy
indicates strong positive or negative correlations between cell types"
(p. 20). A bound makes this precise (our remark). The Shannon entropy
is at least the Rényi entropy of order 2,
$-\log\sum_h\tilde\lambda_h^{2}$, and
$\sum_h\tilde\lambda_h^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{R}_g^{2})/J^{2}$.
With $\overline{\rho^{2}}_g$ the mean squared off-diagonal correlation,

$$
H^{\mathrm{vN}}_g\;\ge\;\log\frac{J}{1+(J-1)\,\overline{\rho^{2}}_g}.
$$ {#eq-fs-vn-renyi}

<!-- chk: V21b -->
Small correlations force a high entropy. A low entropy therefore
requires large correlations on average.

**How Unico uses it.** The entropy stratifies genes for evaluation; it
does not filter them. "Throughout our evaluation of the deconvolution
results, we grouped genes into high- and low-entropy groups", with the
split at the median (p. 20). Fig. 1b shows the normalised entropy over
"the top 10,000 most highly expressed genes in scRNA-seq from PBMC"
(p. 2). On PBMC pseudo-bulks "the improvement of Unico is more pronounced in
genes that exhibit strong cell-type covariance structure (low-entropy
genes; average correlation improvement of 20.0%) compared to
high-entropy genes (average improvement of 14.9%)" (p. 6). Unico keeps
every gene; its benchmark gene sets are random or chosen by variance
(pp. 5, 7, 19). Reading the entropy as a gene filter would go beyond
the paper.

**The analogue for DeCovarT.** DeCovarT treats the cells of different
types as independent, so the $J\times J$ cross-type correlation of a
gene is $\boldsymbol{I}$. Its entropy is the maximum $\log J$ for every
gene, and the criterion carries no information there. Unico's
cross-type covariance is a between-sample quantity: it is closest to
the between-donor covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}$ of
[2.1](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-one-replicate),
extended across types (our remark). The covariance DeCovarT does model
is the within-type covariance across genes. The analogue is then the
entropy @eq-fs-vn-entropy of the $|\mathcal{G}|\times|\mathcal{G}|$
within-type correlation $\boldsymbol{R}_j$ of
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$ restricted to the panel, with $J$
replaced by $|\mathcal{G}|$ (our remark). Its exponential
$\exp H^{\mathrm{vN}}(\boldsymbol{R}_j)$ is the effective rank of
$\boldsymbol{R}_j$
[TODO-cite: Roy & Vetterli 2007, The effective rank: a measure of effective dimensionality, EUSIPCO 2007; no key in the bibs]{.highlight}:
it equals $|\mathcal{G}|$ for independent genes and 1 for a single
module of perfectly correlated genes. A low entropy means a few strong
shared modules, hence few effective directions in type $j$.

- **Against $\kappa_2$.** The condition number of @sec-kappa-limits
  uses the two extreme singular values of the mean matrix. The entropy
  uses the whole spectrum of a correlation matrix. Applied to
  $\boldsymbol{R}_j$, $\kappa_2$ flags one near-null direction, and the
  entropy measures how evenly the variance spreads over all directions
  (our remark).
- **Against D-optimality.** $\log\det\boldsymbol{R}_j=\sum_h\log\lambda_h$
  is also a function of the whole spectrum. With the trace fixed at
  $|\mathcal{G}|$, both $\log\det$ and the entropy are largest at
  $\boldsymbol{R}_j=\boldsymbol{I}$ and decrease as the spectrum
  spreads (our remark). This does not make a low entropy bad for
  DeCovarT. The criteria of @sec-optimal-design score the information
  for $\boldsymbol{p}$, not $\boldsymbol{R}_j$, and in the example of
  @fig-dea-design a correlation of $0.8$ raises $\det I$. What separates
  types is the difference between $\boldsymbol{R}_j$ and
  $\boldsymbol{R}_\ell$, which the overlap $\bar\varpi$ of
  @sec-pareto-panel measures; a low entropy in each type is not enough.

The entropy uses no deconvolution fit, so the circularity of
@wrn-fs-circularity does not apply to it (our remark). It still needs
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$ on a shortlist, so it is post hoc
like the other criteria of this section.

### Fisher information for $\boldsymbol{p}$: D-, E- and A-optimality {#sec-optimal-design}

For a panel $\mathcal{G}$, restrict the rows of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and
the rows and columns of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ to $\mathcal{G}$ and
compute $I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p})$ from
[1.2, Eq. for $I(\boldsymbol{p})$](01-2-population-inference.html#sec-fisher-p),
in $J-1$ free coordinates $\boldsymbol\theta$ with
$\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{p}_0+\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol\theta$.

<!-- chk: V4d -->
For $J=2$ the information is a scalar. Under the single-cell model with
a common within-type covariance it is
$n_i\boldsymbol\Delta^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W^{-1}\boldsymbol\Delta$,
$\boldsymbol\Delta=\boldsymbol\mu_{\cdot1}-\boldsymbol\mu_{\cdot2}$, the
squared Mahalanobis distance between the two type means, as in the
CardamomOT comparison note (section "DeCovarT"); every criterion below
then ranks panels by that distance. From $J=3$ on,
$I_{\mathcal{G}}$ is a matrix and the criteria differ. Because
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$ depends on $\boldsymbol{p}$, a
panel is scored over a composition grid $\mathcal{P}\subset\Delta^{J-1}$
(balanced, rare-type, sparse and near-collinear compositions), and the
classical criteria [@atkinsonOptimumExperimentalDesigns1992;
@pukelsheimOptimalDesignExperiments2006] become

$$
\max_{\mathcal{G}}\min_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathcal{P}}
\log\det I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p})
\ \text{(robust D)},
\qquad
\max_{\mathcal{G}}\min_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathcal{P}}
\lambda_{\min}\bigl(I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr)
\ \text{(E)},
\qquad
\min_{\mathcal{G}}\max_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathcal{P}}
\operatorname{tr}I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}
\ \text{(A)}.
$$ {#eq-optimal-design}

D-optimality shrinks the volume of the confidence ellipsoid for
$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ and can leave one weak contrast; E-optimality
shortens its longest axis, the worst contrast; A-optimality minimises
the average variance.

<!-- chk: V18c -->
The D-ranking does not depend on the basis $\boldsymbol{K}$, since
$\det I_{\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{B}}=(\det\boldsymbol{B})^2\det I_{\boldsymbol{K}}$.
The E- and A-rankings do: they are basis-free only when computed on
$\operatorname{Cov}\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=\boldsymbol{K}I_{\boldsymbol{K}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{K}^{\top}$,
which amounts to an orthonormal $\boldsymbol{K}$. In the raw
coordinates $(p_1,p_2)$, which drop the last type, the E-ranking of two
panels can reverse.

**Common covariance.** With $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W$
for every type, the covariance mixture
$\sum_jp_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W$ does not
depend on $\boldsymbol{p}$ and

$$
I_{\mathcal{G}}
=
n_i\,\boldsymbol{K}^{\top}\boldsymbol{M}_{\mathcal{G}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W^{-1}\boldsymbol{M}_{\mathcal{G}}\boldsymbol{K},
$$ {#eq-fs-info-common}

<!-- chk: V18a, V18b -->
with $\boldsymbol{M}_{\mathcal{G}}$ the $|\mathcal{G}|\times J$ matrix
of type means. If $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W=\boldsymbol{I}$,
$I_{\mathcal{G}}=n_i\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}$ with
$\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{M}_{\mathcal{G}}\boldsymbol{K}$:
D-optimality maximises the squared Gram volume of the contrasted mean
columns, and $\kappa_2(I_{\mathcal{G}})=\kappa_2(\boldsymbol{A})^2$, the
criterion of @sec-weighted-kappa.

<!-- chk: V18d -->
**Example.** Take $J=3$ types and two candidate panels of three genes
with unit variances (@fig-dea-design). In panel A the three genes have
type means $(4,2,2)$, $(4,2,0)$ and $(2,1,4)$; in panel B, $(2,4,2)$,
$(0,2,4)$ and $(0,2,3)$. With independent genes, panel A wins on the
three criteria ($n_i=1$, orthonormal $\boldsymbol{K}$:
$\det I=116/3$ against $104/3$, $\lambda_{\min}=3.18$ against $2.76$,
$\operatorname{tr}I^{-1}=23/58$ against $23/52$). A correlation of $0.8$
between genes 1 and 3 of panel A raises $\det I$ to $60$, so D still
prefers A, but lowers $\lambda_{\min}$ to $2.05$ and raises
$\operatorname{tr}I^{-1}$ to $47/90$, so E and A prefer B. The
correlation sharpens one contrast and blurs the other: the ellipse
shrinks in area and lengthens. A univariate screen sees neither change,
since the marginal law of each gene is the same in both cases.

![D-, E- and A-optimal choice between two gene panels ($J=3$ types, three genes each, unit variances, $n_i=25$). (a) 95 % confidence ellipses of $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ on the simplex plane at $\boldsymbol{p}=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$ with independent genes: panel A (blue) against panel B (orange). (b) Correlation $0.8$ between genes 1 and 3 of panel A: its ellipse (blue) is smaller in area but longer; dashed grey, panel A with independent genes. (c) Log advantage of panel A over panel B for each criterion (positive favours A). Numbers: ledger V18d; code: `scripts/figures/fig_03_1_dea_design.R`.](figures/fig_03_1_dea_design.svg){#fig-dea-design fig-alt="Three panels under a formula box. Panels a and b show a triangle for the three-type simplex with two confidence ellipses at its centre. In panel a the blue ellipse of panel A lies inside the orange ellipse of panel B. In panel b the blue ellipse of correlated panel A is thinner but longer than the orange one. Panel c is a dot plot: with independent genes the three criteria D, E and A all favour panel A; with correlated genes D favours A while E and A favour B."}

This objective needs $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$ on the
candidate genes, hence the covariance estimation of
[3.2](03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html) on a shortlist that tier
(ii) has already produced. The search itself (greedy exchange,
NSGA-II) and its settings are in
[S6](S6-feature-screening-scenario.html#sec-pareto-nsga2).

### Pareto search {#sec-pareto-panel}

`AutoGeneS` optimises two mean-only objectives with a genetic algorithm
(@sec-fs-all-vs-all). For DeCovarT the objectives are
$\kappa_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}})$ (mean geometry) and the
average pairwise overlap $\bar\varpi$ of the type laws
$\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)$
restricted to $\mathcal{G}$ [@melnykovMixSimPackageSimulating2012;
@R-MixSim]. The overlap and the other separation measures (Hellinger,
Bhattacharyya, Jeffreys, affine-invariant distance) are defined in
[4.2](04-2-distances-overlap-metrics.html#sec-overlap-tv); unlike the
`AutoGeneS` objectives they use both means and covariances. A Pareto
front of non-dominated panels is reported instead of one weighted score
[@R-mco]; the planned optimiser is NSGA-II via `mco::nsga2()`, with
genes encoded as a mask in $[0,1]^{|\mathcal{G}_0|}$ and thresholded to
a target size.

::: {#nte-pareto-proposal .callout-note}
## A third objective specific to DeCovarT (proposal)

The robust D- or E-criterion of @eq-optimal-design is a third objective,
best used to choose among non-dominated panels. The two kinds of
criteria need not agree: overlap measures how well the type laws can be
told apart, Fisher information how well $\boldsymbol{p}$ can be
estimated. None of the reviewed methods uses the information for
$\boldsymbol{p}$ to choose genes (@tbl-fs-review).
:::

### Seeds and Markov boundaries {#sec-markov-seeds}

A panel can also grow from a few seeds (strong markers, genes with a
large contribution to $I_{\mathcal{G}}$) by their neighbours in a fitted
graphical model of one type. A Markov blanket of gene $g$ is any set
that makes $g$ conditionally independent of the other genes; a Markov
boundary is a minimal blanket. For a positive distribution the boundary
is unique and equals the neighbour set of $g$ in the minimal undirected
I-map [@pearlProbabilisticReasoningIntelligent1988;
@kollerProbabilisticGraphicalModels2009]. In a Gaussian graphical model
these are the genes $g'$ with $\omega_{gg'}\ne0$ in $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$
[@bolinExplicitLinkGraphical2026], *if* the fitted graph is taken as the
minimal I-map. The construction uses undirected separation; directed
$d$-separation, with its colliders, belongs to DAGs and is a different
operation (@fig-u-vs-dsep). Boundary expansion can reintroduce collinear
means, so the expanded set returns to the Pareto stage.

![Undirected Markov boundary versus directed Markov blanket: left, neighbours of target $g$ in a GGM; right, parents, children and spouses in a DAG under $d$-separation.](figures/markov_boundary_vs_dseparation.png){#fig-u-vs-dsep}

Genes that change neighbourhood between types (differential networks,
`INDEED`, D-trace, cooperative penalties) are a further source of
candidates. Their theory is in
[3.3, joint and differential networks](03-3-precision-networks.html#sec-grn-joint);
on one specimen their permutation nulls are technical nulls
(@wrn-fs-estimand).

## Continuous states {#sec-continua}

Many tissues, gastruloids included, are continua rather than discrete
types. A $J$-column signature is then a piecewise approximation of an
archetype geometry [@hartInferringBiologicalTasks2015] or a potency
axis [@gulatiSinglecellTranscriptionalDiversity2020], and the
condition number of the means is large by construction
(@sec-kappa-limits). Scores along inferred latent axes, and Fisher
information evaluated on continuous components, are open directions;
hierarchical panels (lineage, then subtype) remain the pragmatic choice
[@wangBulkTissueCell2019].

## Mechanistic priors {#sec-mechanistic}

Prior-knowledge networks can annotate a statistically chosen panel or
add soft coverage constraints. `CARNIVAL` contextualises a prior network
from expression footprints by integer programming
[@liuFromExpressionFootprints2019]; `CORNETO` estimates a shared backbone
plus type-specific edges across samples
[@rodriguezMierUnifyingMultisample2025]. Their outputs depend on the
prior network and are hypotheses; they do not replace the criteria of
@sec-fs-multivariate. CardamomOT makes the same point about its own
input: the selected gene set acts as prior information (Maugé & Ventre
2026, p. 27).


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Appendix: concentration results in MEAD and DECALS {#sec-fs-appendix .appendix}

**MEAD.** MEAD's asymptotics are of another kind than those of
@sec-fs-five-bounds. Its central limit theorem runs across genes
($G\to\infty$), not across cells, under local dependence: the noise of
most genes forms a dependency graph of bounded degree (Assumption 4,
PDF p. 11) [@xieStatisticalInferenceCell2026]. The normal approximation
is "Theorem 2.7 of Chen and Shao" (Lemma S4, supplement pp. S16–S17,
PDF pp. 46–47) (Chen & Shao 2004)
[TODO-cite: Chen & Shao 2004, Normal approximation under local dependence, Ann. Probab. 32(3A):1985-2028; no key in the bibs]{.highlight}.

::: {#lem-fs-chen-shao}
## Normal approximation under local dependence

For $W=\sum_{g\in M}Z_g$ with $\operatorname{E}W^2=1$,
$\operatorname{E}Z_g=0$, $\operatorname{E}\lvert Z_g\rvert^{\nu}\le\vartheta^{\nu}$
and maximal degree $d_{\max}$, MEAD prints
$\sum_z\lVert\mathbb{P}(W\le z)-\Phi(z)\rVert\le75\,d_{\max}^{5(\nu-1)}\lvert M\rvert\,\vartheta^{\nu}$.
As printed, the range of $\nu$ is not stated, and a supremum over $z$
is presumably meant.
:::

Assumption 5b (PDF p. 11) asks for uniformly
bounded moments of order above 4 of the bulk data, the reference data
and the platform ratios. Fourth moments are more than a central limit
theorem for a mean needs: MEAD's estimator and its sandwich variance
contain products of noise terms, and the proof bounds their covariances
(PDF p. 40), which takes fourth moments. RNA-Sieve, by contrast, needs a
finite per-cell variance for its central limit theorem across cells,
and boundedness for its tail.

**DECALS.** Theorem 1 of DECALS assumes that the noise terms
of the bulk "are sub-exponential random variables" and states that
this "includes the negative binomial distribution that is often used to
model read counts from RNA-seq data" [@caiStatisticalInferenceCelltype2024,
supplement p. 22]. The paper gives no derivation; @eq-fs-nb-mgf supplies
one. Its Lemma S3 (supplement p. 23) is property (ii) of
@nte-fs-subexp: the moments of a mean-zero sub-exponential variable
satisfy $(\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert^{\nu})^{1/\nu}\le\eta_2\nu$
for all $\nu\ge1$. Eq. S15 (supplement p. 26) applies Lemma S3 to the
scaled noise $Z_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}\xi_{gi}/\sqrt{\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert}$,
with $\xi_{gi}$ the noise of gene $g$ in bulk $i$ and
$\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert$ the number of signature genes:
$\operatorname{E}\lvert Z_{gj}\rvert^{\nu}\le\bigl(\eta_2\tilde\mu_{gj}\,\nu/\sqrt{\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert}\bigr)^{\nu}$
for every $\nu\ge2$. This moment bound feeds their central limit
theorem across genes, Lemma S4, the same result as
@lem-fs-chen-shao. DECALS's norm in Lemma S2 is the moment form
$\sup_{\nu\ge1}\nu^{-1}(\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert^{\nu})^{1/\nu}$,
the smallest $\eta_2$ of property (ii). It equals @eq-fs-psi1 up to an
absolute factor. DECALS cites the equivalences as "Proposition 2.7.1 in
Vershynin (2018)", the first edition; the numbering in @nte-fs-subexp
follows the second edition.

**Dependent genes (Zhang & Li).** DECALS's Lemma S2 (supplement p. 23)
is Theorem 1 of Zhang & Li, cited as a 2022 preprint
[TODO-cite: Zhang & Li, Bernstein inequality for dependent sub-exponential variables on a dependency network, J. Comput. Graph. Stat., doi:10.1080/10618600.2024.2421246 (cited by DECALS as the 2022 preprint arXiv:2205.10672); the theorem number in the published version is still to be checked]{.highlight}.

::: {#thm-fs-zhang-li}
## Bernstein inequality on a dependency graph

For $\lvert M\rvert$ dependent mean-zero sub-exponential $Y_g$ with
dependency graph $\mathcal{H}=(M,\mathcal{E})$, an edge joining two
dependent variables, maximal degree $d_{\max}$ and $\bar\chi_G$ of
@eq-fs-colouring,

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\sum_{g\in M}Y_g\ge t\Bigr)
\le
\bar\chi_G\exp\Bigl[-\gamma\min\Bigl\{\frac{t^{2}}{\bar\chi_G^{2}\sum_{g}\lVert Y_g\rVert_{\psi_1}^{2}},\ \frac{t}{\bar\chi_G\max_g\lVert Y_g\rVert_{\psi_1}}\Bigr\}\Bigr].
$$ {#eq-fs-bernstein-dep}

With no edge, $d_{\max}=0$, $\lvert\mathcal{E}\rvert=0$ and
$\bar\chi_G=1$: the one-sided form of @eq-fs-bernstein (our remark). A
gene network of bounded degree, as DECALS assumes in its Theorem 1,
costs a constant factor in the prefactor and in the exponent. In the
module of @sec-fs-five-bounds, $\bar\chi_G=\min(7,8.26)=7$. Unlike
@thm-fs-nb-dep, this bound keeps the unknown absolute constant
$\gamma$, so it gives the shape of the module tail but no threshold.
:::
